items.body: By the third instalment of their Is Noise series, TAKAAT [pronounced tuh-cot and meaning “noise” in the Tuareg language Tamashek] have moved further from the raw collision of Tuareg guitar and punk that initially defined the project. The trio has become a duo here, without Souleymane Ibrahim’s live drums or any vocals. Vol. 3 is more exploratory and searching, less concerned with songs than with seeing how far Ahmoudou Madassane and Mikey Coltun can stretch their shared musical language. Drum machines, drones and field recordings move into the space left behind. The four-part Ijit N’elwan begins almost by withholding TAKAAT altogether. “Ijit N’elwan 1” opens with field recordings and remains a brief, ambient introduction, establishing a sense of place before amplification takes over. The second part strips things down to an extended, heavily distorted guitar passage whose sustained tones eventually push the track into drone territory. “Ijit N’elwan 3” initially reveals something bluesier in Madassane’s playing, but gradually acquires greater weight and distortion as it progresses, while the final part heads somewhere more psychedelic. Coltun’s comments in the accompanying interview help explain why this expansion feels natural. He draws a connection between the trance-like repetition at the heart of Tuareg guitar music and drone, as well as between the distortion of contemporary Takamba—music blasted through overloaded radios and megaphone speakers—and the punk, noise and experimental music that shaped his own listening. On Vol. 3, those affinities no longer need to be announced: they have become part of the music’s vocabulary. There is also a deliberate sense of risk. Each new TAKAAT EP enters a different world while remaining recognisably part of the same universe, and Vol. 3 takes that idea further than its predecessors. The duo format makes the music feel simultaneously more exposed and more open-ended as well as restless and unafraid of charting new territory. To make sense of the noise we reached out directly to TAKAAT with Mikey Coltun answering our questions. Across the three Is Noise volumes, TAKAAT has moved quite quickly from the raw Tuareg guitar and punk energy of Vol. 1, through the live-to-tape Tinariwen reworkings of Vol. 2, to the drones, drum machines, field recordings and much denser noise of Vol. 3. Was this evolution something you imagined when TAKAAT began, or has each volume simply opened up possibilities for the next one? Mikey Coltun: It’s been a mix of both. We knew there was a lot to explore sonically when Ahmoudou and I started the band but to what extent was a bit more unknown until we started touring and experimenting both live and during the recording process. Each Is Noise is recorded to tape. That’s kinda the overall concept. Similarly if you look at the album art (shout out to our designer Can Misirlioglu) throughout the volumes the structure remains the same but is a different perspective and zoomed out throughout each volume. This was intentional from the beginning as it relates to the music and the progression of each Is Noise volume. Mikey, you’ve drawn a connection between the distortion of modern Takamba—particularly the tehardent amplified through blown-out radios—and the noise and experimental music you grew up with in Washington, D.C. [Andy Downing, Matter News, 4 March 2026]. On Vol. 3, do those traditions actually meet in the way you make sound, or are they still distinct references that you bring into TAKAAT from different directions? Mikey Coltun: There’s definitely all of those influences – Takamba, punk, noise and experimental music present on Vol. 3. Similar to later era John Coltrane, a lot of Tuareg music is drone music at its core. With Tuareg guitar music, a simple chord structure with trance-like rhythms and melodies often played for long periods of time is no different than the spirituality of drone music and this is something Ahmoudou and I were interested in exploring. Taking our guitar and bass and blasting it through amps creating different sonic distortions can be also heard when seeing Takamba music live but instead of the guitar amps you have a blown out radio receiver roaring through megaphone speakers. As Ahmoudou has put it, TAKAAT is the “feeling of being in the desert at night.” Vol. 3 also changes the basic instrumental architecture of TAKAAT: drum machines, drone synths and manipulated field recordings become central alongside Ahmoudou’s guitar and Mikey’s bass. What interested you about moving away from the more recognisable guitar/bass/drums setup of the earlier volumes, and how did that change the way you approached improvisation? Mikey Coltun: It’s important for Ahmoudou and I to be experimenting musically and taking risks. We talk a lot about how Taureg legends Tinariwen pushed, what Tuareg music is, and what we’re doing with TAKAAT is breaking the expectations of the known Tuareg rock sound. We want each record to push into a different world while still staying in the universe of TAKAAT. This goes the same with our shows. Each tour Ahmoudou and I want to present something different with TAKAAT. The first few tours we did the trio, last tour was a duo presenting a loud drone and blown out drum machines, and next tour will be something different too. We’re taking risks and we want people to come take these risks with us. This is the only way to push out of comfort zones and create something new. You’ve described the trust developed through eight years of playing together as something that allows TAKAAT to take risks, while Mikey has also spoken about the project as a return to a more DIY world where there is less pressure to perform in a particular way [Andy Downing, Matter News, 4 March 2026]. Does TAKAAT give you a kind of freedom that you don’t necessarily have in Mdou Moctar—and has that freedom changed the way you listen and respond to one another when you play? Mikey Coltun: It was really clear early on touring together with Mdou Moctar that Ahmoudou and I were excited by similar music. I brought a lot of different types of bands on tour with Mdou. All of the music is by groups and artists that I love. While some of the groups could have been challenging to listeners it was important to me to draw that connection with what we were doing with Mdou. Mdou’s music was different and challenging to some in the Tuareg wedding scene in Agadez, Niger. With a lot of these bands I brought on tour I found Ahmoudou’s interest peaked. Whenever there was an opportunity on tour I would take him to see sound installations, free jazz groups, modern art, etc… and he really does appreciate that. Because Ahmoudou and I have similar interests sonically, there is a lot of trust and comfortability to experiment and try new things together with TAKAAT. (Gianmarco Del Re)

items._cn_summary: TAKAAT的《Is Noise》第三卷由三重奏缩减为双人组合，放弃了实鼓和人声，转而引入鼓机、嗡鸣音与环境录音，向更广阔的声响空间探索。四乐章《Ijit N'elwan》从纯粹的环境白描起始，逐步过渡到失真吉他长音构成的嗡鸣地带，第三段浮现蓝调吉他语汇并逐渐加重失真，末段则走向迷幻深处。乐队从图阿雷格吉他与朋克的原始碰撞出发，经由对Tinariwen的现场录音重制，最终抵达密集噪音与嗡鸣音交织的领域。每张EP都进入一个不同世界却仍属同一宇宙，第三卷将这一理念推至更远——双人编制使音乐同时显得更为裸露和开放，充满冒险意识。这张专辑全部以磁带录制，将图阿雷格吉他音乐中恍惚般的重复性与嗡鸣音传统相连，承载了独特的撒哈拉文化视角。

items.body:
Curating a retrospective of 40 years of recorded music is a daunting task, particularly when it is your own. Accurately representing the arc of the work and the life that created it requires frankness and acceptance. It is a process punctuated with winces and sighs and the occasional grin. Composer and improviser Jin Hi Kim experienced it all when compiling The Jin Hi Kim Collection, recently issued by Neuma. If the use of “odyssey” requires a great voyage, discovering new lands, and encountering titans, then Kim’s journey easily qualifies. Not only did she leave Korea at 23 for the US in 1980, Kim traversed an arguably greater gulf by leaving her elite training in traditional Korean music to study electronic music and composition with Lou Harrison, Terry Riley, and others. In the intervening decades, she worked with leading exponents of contemporary composition and improvisation like Kronos Quartet and Derek Bailey, and transformed the komungo, the traditional five-foot-long lute dating from the 4th Century CE, exponentially extending its sonic range through computer interfaces and signal processing.

Rediscovery accompanied the selection process for the 9-CD Collection. She was especially surprised when reviewing early works transliterating Korean music through Western instruments, or employing graphic notation. “It was created by a young mind,” Kim recently recalled with a laugh. “Sometimes it was hard to hear that’s what I did. But it was also good evidence for an archival collection. It was a wonderful feeling to look at everything I did – well, almost everything – but one thing that I was really proud about it is that there is not just one kind of music. Each piece has its Korean roots but, like I’ve said, I came to America to make new music, so I look at my 40 years of work and, yeah, I achieved that. So, it was a very satisfying process.

“When I listen to some of the improvisations, I realized how young and unafraid I was. Komungo has a limited sound compared to other instruments. When you work with virtuoso improvisers, they have vocabularies that are so rich. They are creating so many different colors and textures, but komungo has limits. It doesn’t allow you to express so much of the story. It has a meditative energy, of nothingness, of slowness. I was so brave to use this instrument with such incredible masters and to communicate with them and create music with them. I did it somehow with my inner energy. I was able to present this inner energy.”

The Collection almost equally divides Kim’s work in composition and improvisation, with five discs devoted to works for orchestra and chamber music ensembles, and four documenting improvisations with, among others, an impressive diversity of percussionists, including Gerry Hemingway, Susie Ibarra, and Tony Oxley, and string players like Bill Frisell, Min Xiao-Fen, and Hans Reichel. If anything can be read into it, the slight tilt reflects her ardent pursuit to articulate the concept of Living Tones Compositions, and how central it is to her work.

“The most important thing about the Living Tones Compositions is to convey the Korean element and philosophy through Western contemporary music,” she explained. “When I came to the United States after training in traditional Korean music, European classical music was more respected in Korea than the traditional music. They didn’t know much about American avant-garde music then, in the 1970s. I was a young musician who trained with the very best teachers and saw that I was not respected because I was not doing Western music.

“That created within me a great desire to fix that problem. You can’t fix anything, but I was young, I had a passion and a mission. I was living in the United States; I was composing for Western musicians; so how could I make this Korean idea, this Korean state of mind in making music, how could I put this together with Western music with equal respect? That was my thing. All my Living Tones Compositions come from the idea of putting together the Korean context and philosophy and Western instruments and musical context, to see how Western musicians took to the Korean attitude – not necessarily techniques, scales, anything like that – but this attitude, this state of mind. That’s what I’m doing with Living Tones music.

“Korean traditional music was once influenced by Chinese music,” Kim prefaced to explain the context and philosophy of Korean music, which she also detailed extensively in her book, Duality of Ancient Korean Roots and Western New Music. “Korean music can be divided into folk music and court music. Court music was quite different from music of ordinary people. The court was deeply influenced by ancient Chinese philosophy – yin and yang; the five elements, and ancient ancestors worship. The music wasn’t entertainment; it was ritual – that was part of both court and folk music. For ordinary people, they associated music with the shaman. For court music, there were virtuoso musicians who created an austere music, based on a philosophy of cosmic sound and abstract thinking; but for ordinary people, the shaman always took care of pain, community pain. Music was performed for celebrations of harvests and other things, but more for problems like drought, someone who is sick, some kind of problem. The shaman is always dealing with the problem of pain in their lives. They always had to sing something very sad. Her song has nothing to do with joyous things – always grief and pain. Ordinary people related to that.

“Both court and folk music had an emphasis on energy – they never thought of music as just sound. It had healing energy. In the folk community, they tried to imitate the shaman, the way she sang, shaking the notes, trying to reach out to another spirit, trying to connect heaven and earth. If you listen to a shaman’s song, there’s a very strong vibrato. The instrumentalists who don’t sing listen to this type of music; it’s very touching, very soulful, and it reflects the problems in their lives. Korean instrumentalists are all shaking, shaking their hands, shaking their instruments, shaking their notes. I play komungo, where the strings can move a lot, up and down, so you can really shake the notes and express the music in the same way as the shaman. I translate that process, that context, that spirit, into Living Tones. Each tone has its own light, and because it has its own light, its time is elastic. It is not like abstract Western time, where you count the time of each note perfectly, and you don’t have the space for microtones. There’s no time to do that in Western music. Time becomes much more open and that’s why in Korean music they don’t talk about abstract time but time in a cycle. Within that cycle, you have a lot of freedom of how to use that space with deep vibratos or any other articulation to create that intense feeling.”

The qualities Kim ascribes to Korean music are manifest in the komungo. It has a palpably plangent sound, with a bass register lower and more resonant than the guembri’s and the sting of ancient harps in its highest notes. It has a timbral luster comparable to the dark, iridescent glazes of pit-fired ceramics or the blocks of deep color that hover over the black basecoats of a Mark Rothko painting. Its dredge-like twang and the skeletal figures central to the music stop the racing, associative Western mind dead in its tracks. Even before Kim augmented the instrument with signal processing, Western improvisers had a strong attraction to the komungo. Conversely, improvisation has, over the decades, impacted Kim’s outlook.

However, Kim has a nuanced view on how improvisation has influenced her. “Influence is the result over a long period,” she elaborated, “because I played with a person one time or two times. That long period is a really deep space. It’s not that a particular musician gave me something. It is that the experience of playing with someone becomes part of my life experience. Now I look at something differently than when I was young. I understand how the universe works because of scientists and I understand how improvisation works because of improvisers. When you travel all around the world – I’ve performed in over 60 countries and have lived in some of these countries for a long time, six months or even a year – then you have an incredibly different life perspective. All of those things interest me. So, I have been influenced by many things over the decades, so that when I play with someone, it is not just that moment I am responding to; it’s everything about the other musicians: their instruments; their traditions; their culture. That gives me a very clear idea what to do.

“When I was young, I was so desperate to communicate successfully with each improviser I played with. I was trying to understand their personality; I was trying to understand their vocabulary. There have been very few times that I played on the spot without any information about the people I was playing with. I had heard them before I had the opportunity to play with them, playing with other musicians or solo. In my own way, I understood who they are. If I don’t understand them and their musical elements, I have no way to contribute anything on komungo. I have to understand their personality, their energy, how they process the music. Not all people process the same way; some people are poetic; some people are very emotional; some people are very funny. Everybody has those things happening. Understanding that was very important to me. It helped me to communicate, to hear what they were giving me, so I could give back. I listened a lot to what they were doing at a particular moment.”

Given that improvisers spanning James Newton and Elliott Sharp, and Rüdiger Carl and Oliver Lake, are heard throughout the box set, it is noteworthy that Kim singles one out to illustrate her approach to improvisation. “When I work with William Parker, he has a very deep energy in his soul,” she said of the bassist. “When I played with him, he influenced me with his deep energy. It’s really big. That influenced me to be really big. That bigness, that abundance, that tireless energy; that lets us play a really long time. He has the qualities to do something that a Korean shaman could do, playing the same idea over and over and over for a long time – trance like – but the energy becomes more powerful. William Parker has that type of energy. The bass is like the komungo; it has a deep energy and incredible power. I’m really influenced by that.”

Retrospectives like the Collection are generally considered to be merely summations, but in Kim’s case, it is more a marker of distance travelled and journeys ahead. “It reflects my continuous evolution as an artist. Throughout my musical journey, I have always searched for new ways to express myself creatively while remaining deeply rooted in my Korean musical identity.

“In essence, every work in this collection is the result of my enduring desire to elevate often-neglected Korean aesthetics, shaped alongside the freedom I found in America – a place that allowed me to pursue my artistic passions and ideas without limitation.

“Today, my perspective extends beyond national boundaries to the increasingly interconnected global community. I have aspired to use music as a spiritual and transformative force to confront social challenges. I believe this has become the new direction of my artistic journey.”

Kim’s new direction has steered her towards to uplifting marginalized subalterns and breaking through the fourth wall of the concert hall separating musicians from listeners. “Right now, because the world has changed so much, and America is now so blue, and so many people are mentally ill – I know because I recently gave a music meditation workshop at the Yale mental health center – I want to do something about community pain. I always go back to what the shaman does. I think I have sort of achieved my goal of blending Korean and Western ways of thinking with Living Tones, so right now I want to make music that the community participates in. Not necessarily well-trained musicians, but anybody who is interested. I already started on this in 2023 with a piece called ‘Ritual for Earth.’ I would like to do these things for now. I’m not anxious about my career or my next commission. I’m thinking about community pain, environmental issues like wildfires and floods, the world we are living in. So, if I have the opportunity, working with communities is what I want to do.”

items._cn_summary: 这张9CD合辑回顾了韩裔作曲家兼即兴演奏家Jin Hi Kim四十年的创作生涯，发行于Neuma厂牌。她从韩国传统音乐出发，赴美后转向电子音乐与作曲，师从Lou Harrison和Terry Riley，并将拥有四千年历史的韩国传统乐器杖筝（komungo）通过计算机接口和信号处理大幅拓展其声音表现力。合辑五张碟收录管弦乐与室内乐作品，四张碟记录她与Gerry Hemingway、Bill Frisell、Susie Ibarra、Tony Oxley等即兴大师的合作。音乐跨越传统韩国音乐与西方乐器、图形记谱、电子手段之间的界限，融合冥想性的内在能量与自由即兴的丰富语汇，展现了一位跨文化艺术家对传统器乐在当代语境中可能性的持续探索。

items.body: While much of Grisha Shakhnes’ music could be categorised as obscure and undifferentiated, “The distance between a word and a deed” strikes me as perhaps his most elusive effort yet. (It’s also his longest, clocking in at around two hours if you count the bonus material included with the download.) This elusiveness makes me think of the monochrome paintings of artists such as Robert Rauschenberg and Ad Reinhardt — blank and featureless at first glance, but on closer inspection a subtle wealth of detail emerges from the traces of brushstrokes or the uneven application of paint. Shakhnes’ music has such hidden details too: the long, terrifying crescendo in ‘Stockholm variation #2.5’ and the quiet opening to ‘Stockholm variation #3’ are two of the more prominent examples. Indeed, after multiple listens the various whoops, rumbles, crackles, whistles, and distortions heard across the album could hardly be called ‘undifferentiated’ in any strict sense, but what is interesting is that the sense of blankness and elusiveness remains, even after the details have become audible. It’s as if the album invited (at least) two equally valid and rewarding ways of listening: you can zoom in on the subtle nuances and changing timbres, or you can let the quietly thundering, rattling flow carry you away from all concepts and all thought. In the latter mode, the music acts on the senses like a heavy downpour or the constant chugging of a train. Both ways of listening are rewarding, and can be switched between at will. Yet however one listens, there’s a vague sense of melancholy or restlessness that hangs in the air like a mist, preventing things from becoming too comfortable. This is not some kind of ganzfeld effect, creating a uniform stimulation field to trick the senses; rather, there’s the perception (hallucination?) of a certain turning away, a declining to comment, a silence that is allowed to fall behind and between the rumble and clatter. Sometimes the distance between a word and a deed can be very great. the distance between a word and a deed by Grisha Shakhnes Grisha Shakhnes / Disappearing Records

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑时长约两小时，以极度模糊和难以捉摸的整体气质著称。评论者将其比作罗伯特·劳森伯格和阿德·赖因哈特等人的单色画作——乍看空无一物、毫无特征，但反复聆听后，细节逐渐浮现：悠长而惊悚的渐强、安静的开场，以及遍布全片的呼啸、低鸣、噼啪、口哨和失真。两种聆听方式并存：聚焦于微妙音色变化的近距离凝视，或让低沉轰鸣的声流席卷感官。专辑始终笼罩着一层模糊的忧郁与不安，既非纯粹的感觉剥夺效应，也并非完全沉默，而是介于声响之间的留白与回避。评论指出言语与行动之间的距离有时极为遥远，这恰恰映射了音乐本身的姿态。

items.body: Thematically, Post Dub Cities hearkens back to Future Sound of London’s Dead Cities, while tonally it recalls Murcof’s Rememberanza. Adriano Zanni‘s vision of a future world is the cold reflection of a present reality in which many places are already deserted: peeling houses, dilapidated storefronts, bombed villages. At one time, they teemed with life. Once humans have no more use for a city, they abandon it, leaving only rubble and questionable specters. The reasons may be as far afield as the loss of jobs, the evaporation of resources, or a campaign of bombs. More than anything, Post Dub Cities is an album of mood. Zanni wants his listeners to be uncomfortable, to regard these cities as one does the stone wreckage of Ozymandius. From the opening notes of “Crisopoli” (also the first single), he casts a spell of resignation and despair. The pace is slow, but not sluggish; the beats restrained, but not soft. Someone has to bear witness. In “Pyramiden,” the tone grows harsher, with amplified whispers, clacking pipes and cavernous echoes. Were it not for the dub timbres, one might call this industrial or post-industrial music. Each piece seems to hide another piece behind it: a subdued rhythm, a moving shadow. In “Centralia,” sharp beats stumble like scavengers sifting through wreckage. These visitors may not be human, or even humanoid; in Alan Weisman’s classic The World Without Us, everything from roaches to raccoons reclaims its own. Rust abrades metal; girders bend; branches break through glass. The accompanying pdf is essential to the release. Referencing Calvino and Marcelli, Zanni writes of the empty city as an “echo chamber,” an image reflected in the music. A hundred pages of sublime black and white photographs follow, captured in cities around the world over the past two decades. The unifying feature is the lack of any human presence, as if scrubbed from existence (insert sci-fi theory here). Proof of humanity’s presence remains, but without context. In Zanni’s own words: “memory without recollection, structure without use, body without inhabitants.” In response, the music is architectural: one imagines a grid in which beats and notes are purposely placed. Belgrade, Vienna, Amsterdam, Barcelona, Berlin, Dublin, Sarajevo, Rome, London, Prague, Madrid, Krakow, Istanbul, Lisbon, Palermo and more, all deserted: buildings empty, rollercoasters stilled, markets abandoned, art left to dissolve. Not a single vehicle is visible, even on the highway. One can see what humans have done, but not where they have gone. In what seems to be the final image, a massive wall of chairs is ready for a group of patrons who never arrive. Capturing these images must have required remarkable patience and timing. The last bonus track, “San Zhi Pod City,” offers a surprise: the appearance of a human voice. Even this turns out to be a loop, a remnant, an echo. But Zanni does have a final trick up his sleeve: on page 99, the people reappear, filling the square. The last four images show humanity wall to literal wall: perhaps too much humanity, suggesting a reason for its removal or demise. As much as one pores through “Kadykchan” and “San Zhi Pod City” for a matching restoration, one cannot hear it in the grooves. The listener is left to ponder whether the detritus of humanity might hold any intrinsic value, or if it is only sound and fury, signifying nothing. (Richard Allen)

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑以未来城市废墟为核心意象，将dub音色与后工业电子融合，构建出缓慢而压迫的声场。配器上运用放大耳语、金属敲击与空旷回响模拟空城回廊，节奏克制但带有侵略性的不规则脉动。专辑附带一本黑白摄影集，跨越二十年拍摄全球废弃城市——建筑残留人类痕迹却无人存在，构成视觉与听觉的双重叙事。声音被形容为'记忆却无回忆，结构却无用处，身体却无居住者'的声学对应物，呈现出网格化、架构式的音乐思维。从开篇到末尾的彩蛋人声loop，整张专辑如同一场关于人类消失后的声音考古，将dub的深沉空间感推向更冷峻、更荒凉的实验边界。

items.body: In a house in Lomé, a woman kept a set of ceremonial pots she used for preparing potions for the older women of the Vodun temples. Vodun is the West African religion the Ewe and Fon have practised across Togo and Benin for centuries, the one that crossed the Atlantic on slave ships and became Haitian Vodou and Louisiana Voodoo. Its spirits are bound up with natural forces and they are reached through drumming and singing, so those women sang constantly. Her grandson grew up believing all that singing had gone into the clay and stayed there. Years later he took the pots and built a drum kit out of them. His name is Toto Tchilatchi, and half of what Nana Benz du Togo carry onto a stage is those pots. The other half is a bass David Kasanku built out of PVC drainpipe. He used to play bass, then spent four years assembling the gazé tuyau. Once it went underneath Toto’s kit, the pots and drums came to life, and together they made a groove full of sub-bass and complex polyrhythms. That groove became the bedrock for three singers, Lady Apoc, Parus Kekeli and Izealedu, with a small vintage Korg keyboard alongside their voices. The band’s word for what all of it adds up to is trance. They describe Vodun itself as being about rhythm, trance, nature and connection, and Lady Apoc says theirs comes from “repetitive energy.“ None of the five knew each other until 2019, when Peter Solo, the leader of Vaudou Game, came to Lomé to run a workshop and brought local musicians and artists together for it. Out of that workshop came the band, and Solo has produced them ever since. They took their name from the Nana Benz, the wax-print traders of Lomé’s central market who drove Mercedes-Benz cars and were confided in by the powerful. The band say they admire the courage and force those women showed in patriarchal societies. They sing in English, French and Mina, over the Vodun scales of the snake, Dan, and of Mami Wata, about women and the earth, and they say protecting one is inseparable from protecting the other. Their feminism, the band say, comes from the strength and resilience of African women, and their ecology from Vodun itself, and they say protecting women and protecting the earth cannot be pulled apart. Like many people of their generation, they grew up with mixed feelings about Vodun and were taught to be ashamed of parts of it, and at some point they moved away from it. Going back gave them their voice back. They stopped trying to fit into a musical category and started creating from who they are. Even so, they never set out to put Vodun in the spotlight, and years of work in the shadows came before they dared to get on a stage. Their first concert in Europe was Transmusicales de Rennes in 2022, and AGO followed the year after, recorded at the OTODI studio in Lomé with Solo producing. They went back to OTODI in December 2024 to record SÉ NAM, again with Solo, and it came out in June 2025. Its eleven tracks have a more contemporary production and more room for groove and rhythm. The title means “understand me” in Mina, one of the three languages they sing in. In October they bring it to WOMEX in Las Palmas… For this episode of Musical Road to WOMEX they answered our questions about how Vodun meets the dancefloor, what their handmade instruments do and what they hope to find on the island: they want to hear the timple, meet local musicians and find out what traces of African and Atlantic exchange can still be heard in Canarian music, and they arrive, as they put it, with their ears open. The playlist at the end lets you hear what they are bringing. You’ve been described as pioneers of “digital voodoo”. For someone hearing you for the first time, how would you introduce the meeting of Vodun tradition and the dancefloor? For us, Digital Vodou is not about taking something old and trying to make it modern. It is about showing that Vodun is already alive and has always had the power to evolve. Vodun is about rhythm, trance, nature and connection. And the dancefloor can be a place for that too. People come together, move together, let go. We bring traditional rhythms, songs, percussion and the handmade instruments we create into electronic music, bass and contemporary sounds. For us, it is a meeting between something very old and something that is still being born. That is what makes it feel both ancestral and futuristic. The band takes its name from the Nana Benz, the market women who turned the wax-print trade into power and independence. What did diving back into your Vodun heritage, after leaving it behind, open up for you musically? It gave us our voice back. Like many people from our generation, we grew up with mixed feelings about Vodun. There were things we were taught to be ashamed of, so at some point we moved away from it. Coming back to it changed the way we saw ourselves. We realised that Vodun is not only a spiritual tradition. It is also a way of understanding our relationship with the earth, with women, with our ancestors and with each other. And musically, it opened a whole world for us: rhythms, melodies, stories, symbols. Things that were already inside us. We stopped trying to fit into a musical category. We started creating from who we really are. WOMEX lands this year in Las Palmas de Gran Canaria, an Atlantic island whose own traditions ride on the timple, a five-string guitar that carries both African and Latin American trade routes. What are you most curious to discover there? We are curious about the connections between the different traditions. Islands are special places. Cultures arrive there, meet, change and survive. We want to hear the timple, meet local musicians and discover what traces of African and Atlantic exchanges can still be heard in Canarian music. And honestly, we are excited about the unexpected. Maybe one of our handmade instruments will meet a sound from the island in a way we never imagined. That is what we love about music. Your instruments are handmade and upcycled, the gazé tuyaux among them, and your themes are feminist and ecological. In a WOMEX programme full of traditions, what makes your sound and your message unmistakably yours? For us, everything is connected. The recycled instruments are not just something you see on stage. They are part of our sound and part of the way we think. We take things that people throw away and give them another life. In a way, we do the same with our stories and traditions. We take things that have been misunderstood or pushed aside and bring them back into the present. Our feminism comes from the strength and resilience of African women. And our connection to ecology comes from Vodun itself. We often say, “Whoever does not respect women does not respect nature.” For us, that says a lot about who Nana Benz Du Togo is. WOMEX is built on unexpected meetings. Which artists, labels or collaborators are you hoping to cross paths with in Las Palmas? We don’t really have a list of names. We want to meet people who are deeply connected to where they come from but are not afraid to experiment. Artists who can move between tradition, ritual, electronic music, performance and new ideas. And that is one of the things we love about WOMEX. You can have a conversation with someone backstage and suddenly discover that there is something you can create together. We are coming with our ears open. You’ve toured Europe and built a reputation as a live force. Does a room of delegates and music professionals change how you bring the trance and the groove of your set? Not really. Of course, we know that WOMEX is important and that there will be a lot of professionals in the room. But once we are on stage, we have to be ourselves. Whether there are one hundred people, a thousand people or music professionals watching us, we want the same thing: for people to feel the music in their bodies. We want them to forget for a moment who they are supposed to be and simply become part of the rhythm. That is when the magic happens. “Voodoo is Nature,” you’ve said. Gran Canaria is a volcanic island shaped by the ocean around it. Does a landscape like that speak to the ecology at the heart of your songs? Absolutely. When you see a volcanic landscape, you are reminded that the earth is alive. It is powerful, it changes, it moves. For us, nature is not something outside of us. In Vodun, it is a living presence. The ocean, the wind, the stone, the fire inside the earth, these are not just things around us. They are forces. So being on an island shaped by the ocean and volcanoes feels very familiar to our way of thinking. It reminds us that we are part of something much bigger than ourselves. Your work carries a clear message about women’s strength and respect for the planet. Is there something you feel especially compelled to say through this showcase? Yes. We want to remind people that protecting women and protecting the earth are not separate things. We believe our traditions can still teach us something about that balance. We are not trying to go back to the past. We are trying to understand what we can take from it to imagine a different future. For us, women are creators, transmitters, protectors and forces of transformation. That is something we want to celebrate through our music. After SÉ NAM, what’s next? New recordings, new collaborations, directions you’re keen to push the project toward? SÉ NAM was an important chapter for us, but we already feel the next one coming. We are working on new music and pushing the dialogue between ritual percussion, the instruments we make ourselves and electronic production even further. We also want to work with artists from other parts of Africa, the Caribbean and Latin America. There are so many shared histories, rhythms and spiritual connections across the Atlantic that we would love to explore. We want to keep moving forward without losing our roots. If you could write a personal invitation to the people of Las Palmas to come and discover your showcase, what would it say? Come with your body before your expectations. Come to dance, listen, feel and maybe remember something older than all of us. We are bringing rhythms from Togo, women’s voices, handmade instruments and the energy of Digital Vodou. Don’t just come and watch us. Come and experience it with us. If you join us, we will create the ceremony together.   On 23 October at the Plaza Stage in Las Palmas de Gran Canaria, Nana Benz du Togo will ask the WOMEX crowd to forget for a moment who they are supposed to be and become part of the rhythm   PLAYLIST: NANA BENZ DU TOGO X RHYTHM PASSPORT   You can find all the previous episodes of Musical Road to Womex HERE   The post Musical Road to WOMEX 2026 – Nana Benz du Togo appeared first on Rhythm Passport.

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑来自多哥洛美的Nana Benz du Togo乐队，乐评详细讲述了乐器的独特来源：鼓手Toto Tchilatchi将祖母用于伏都教仪式熬制药剂的陶罐改造成鼓组，贝斯手David Kasanku则用四年时间用PVC排水管手工制作了低音号gazé tuyau。这些非常规乐器结合三位歌手的嗓音和小 vintage Korg键盘，构建出充满次低音和复杂复合节奏的迷幻律动。乐队在Vaudou Game主脑Peter Solo的制作下，于洛美OTODI工作室完成录制，歌曲以英语、法语和米纳语演唱，取材于伏都教蛇神Dan和Mami Wata的神圣音阶，主题围绕女性力量与大地生态的不可分割性。乐队从2022年雷恩Transmusicales音乐节开始走向欧洲舞台，作品扎根于西非宗教传统的回归与重新诠释，将仪式性的反复能量转化为当代世界音乐场景中独具辨识度的声音实践。

items.body: Band: Sigh | Album: Goh-Ka | Genre: Progressive metal | Year: 2026 From: Tokyo, Japan | Label: Peaceville For fans of: Enslaved, Between the Buried and Me, Opeth Bandcamp Sigh is one of the longest-running and most influential progressive metal bands out there. Starting off as a symphonic black metal band in the early 1990s, they quickly took a more experimental turn and never looked back. Goh-Ka is the band’s 14th full-length release (or 13th, if you want to categorize last year’s re-recording of their 2007 album, Hangman’s Hymn, a little differently). This album is based on kusōzu, a Japanese artform depicting the nine stages of decay described in Buddhism. These are used as a means of meditation on impermanence. The music here sticks to Sigh’s usual style. But where the last album of theirs I listened to–Shiki–left me unimpressed, this is one of their strongest outings. Avant-garde, progressive, and Japanese folk elements play large parts on this album, and the use of recurring musical themes ties everything together. Japanese folk was more prominent than usual on Shiki, and that trend continues here. Goh-Ka opens with the nine-minute “Kuso-shi 1, 2, and 3”. Sigh’s signature synth tones weave and burble amid heavy guitar lines, accented with traditional Japanese instrumentation. This cut is relatively restrained by Sigh’s standards, but that degree of focus pays off here. The power of the music is apparent, and the band’s decision to up the Japonic elements helps this to stand out. The shifts between avant-garde metal, organ-fueled prog, and Japanese folk are fluid and organic. “Jigoku-Zoshi 1: Unkamusho” has an anxious opening with some nearly-Latin-sounding percussion. But soon enough it plunges into melodic black metal with speedy synth flourishes and classical-influenced guitar lines. This is classic Sigh, and it’s a lot of fun. Things slow down on “Anzenshokon”. Acoustic guitar, flute, and clean vocals lend this a mournful feel in its opening. Crushing, doomy guitars burst in on occasion to punctuate the verses, and psychedelic production adds a dreamlike quality, all of which do an incredible job at evoking a corpse rotting in a field, but in a reflective way. In the last couple minutes, the band incorporates obvious early King Crimson influences for a dramatic conclusion. “Kuso-shi 4, 5, and 6” comes next, opening with lush, symphonic doom metal tones. The drumming here (and elsewhere on the album) is stellar, with lots of fancy fills and flourishes. A sinister acoustic passage follows this, evoking some of Opeth’s better quiet moments. Themes from parts 1-3 are revisited here, as are the psychedelic acoustic tones of the preceding song, adding a sense of cohesion. I really like the intermingling of electric and acoustic elements. Not only are Japanese instruments used (maybe it’s a shamisen? Or a koto? I’m not sure.), but some Western-style classical guitar shows up, as well. This is a lurching, foreboding composition that highlights all this band’s best tendencies. “Shoso” is an eerie, one-minute electronic instrumental interlude that leads right into “Unputenpu”. This is a savage, biting composition that sees guitar and shamisen harmonizing beneath raving vocals. Melodic moments contrast against this, and Mikael Åkerfeldt of Opeth shows up to provide a solo. I really love the unorthodox percussion choices deployed during the chorus. Some sinister synth and shamisen open up “Jinmenjushen” as the band dips back into some slower riffage. The verses are much more energetic, though, focusing on melodic black metal, sometimes bordering on black ‘n’ roll. There’s a clear sense of drama here with the group vocals during the chorus, and some unexpected saxophone harmonizes with synthesizer during a particularly exciting instrumental break. This is a breakneck composition that hardly takes its foot off the accelerator once things get going. The final minute does slow down a bit, but there’s no lack of intensity. “Jigoku-Zoshi 2: Tokatsujigoku” immediately bursts forth with powerful black metal. The drumming is again a highlight here. The chorus of this song dips into avant-garde orchestral elements. I’d compare this to some of BTBAM’s odder songs, but Sigh’s been doing weird metal for much longer than those guys. A pair of sub-two-minute songs follow. “Kushukankyo” feels Andean, with breathy flute, gently strummed guitar, and understated hand percussion. It’s a wonderful little breather. “Kuso-shi 7”, on the other hand, consists mostly of sound effects and weird synthesizer bloops.  The album closes on its longest song, the 11-minute “Kuso-shi 8 and 9 / Mettaijakujo”. After a dramatic, theatrical opening, the first verse is relatively grounded. Acoustic and electric passages contrast wonderfully. Dashes of electronic and psychedelic music crop up amid the crushing riffs. Plenty of bands throw things together and hope they work; Sigh is one of the bands that best integrates strange inclusions in a way that makes sense. Folk elements, topped with big, melodic guitar lines lead off the second half of this song. More musical themes from earlier in the record are revisited in a satisfying way. Rock elements eventually melt away altogether as this piece enters its final movement. Orchestral music takes over in a macabre march, eventually dissolving into a synthesizer drone. After some warbling static, the album ends on a warm and peaceful electric piano passage, underscoring the overall concept of this album: accepting the impermanence of life. Goh-Ka is another excellent work from Sigh. Everything here is lively and played with so much passion. The band does an amazing job at varying tempo and texture, and their ability to change direction so suddenly and skillfully is always impressive. Score: 96/100
items._genre: progressive metal / avant-garde / Japanese folk / experimental metal
items._cn_summary: Sigh 乐队的新作以日本佛教艺术“九相图”为概念基础，将尸体腐败的九个阶段转化为冥想素材，在前卫金属框架中大量融入日本传统器乐与民谣元素。专辑由相互呼应的主题动机串联，前卫金属、管风琴驱动的复古前卫段落与日式器乐之间实现流畅转换。合成器音色贯穿始终，与重型吉他交织，形成乐队一贯的实验金属美学。部分曲目结合拉丁风格打击乐与旋律黑金属，段落之间频繁切换轻重缓急，另一些曲目则以原声吉他与笛声铺陈忧郁氛围，后期引入毁灭性段落与早期 King Crimson 式的影响。整体呈现出东方生死观与现代前卫金属的独特融合，是乐队近年最具完成度的作品之一。

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — Right off the bat, playing the harmonium like a classical piano hints at the atypical nature of this album. Five Suns is like an explosion containing multiple explosions within itself, much like fireworks that conceal other pyrotechnics, releasing them at just the right moment. Guitar and organ flesh out the trio's sound, which surges forward with the Mellotron in Part 2 of the Five Suns suite.We are talking about the English band Guapo; they constantly shift and mutate, yet their musical vision remains consistently compelling and challenging, both for the musicians themselves and for the listener. Perhaps therein lies the secret: while their previous album, Great Sage, Equal of Heaven, was a duo featuring a guest saxophonist, here, as a stripped-down trio, they sound richer and darker. They evoke a King Crimson-esque vibe infused with dissonant jazz-rock, while also bringing to mind the dense fusion of the Norwegian band Red Kite and the psychedelic space rock of Monomith.The fact that both Matt Thompson and Daniel O'Sullivan alternated between guitar and samplers, while Dave Smith varied the drum rhythms, contributed to the suite's unpredictability. This was followed by subtle moments of counterpoint between the bass and the Rhodes, which in turn served as a foundation for new drum solos; the drums never stood alone for long, however, before the guitar rejoined the mix. Just when the balance seemed to tip toward Mahavishnu-style fusion, that compulsion for avant-garde composition returned, defining the entirety of Part 3 of Five Suns, as dissonance and psychedelia took center stage.Another key point for me was their ability to know exactly when to break up repetitive sections with rhythm changes; every element had its own purpose and appeared at precisely the right moment. There is room for groove in Five Suns, just as at other moments chaos takes over and things spiral out of control, a chaos that ultimately proves to be controlled, much like improvisation in classic jazz, a passage that highlights precisely the strength of the other."Five Suns," Part 4, with its more prominent organ and contrapuntal drumming, sounds more progressive and thrilling, building to a near-dramatic climax reminiscent of Yndi Halda's Enjoy Eternal Bliss. The fifth and final part carries an aura of danger and suspense; as the distorted guitar gives way to the keyboards, the music plunges into the void of an organ solo lost in an unfathomable abyss."Mictlan" possesses the freshness, lightness, and fluidity of a unique piece, as if casting off the heavy burden of belonging to such a dense suite; the Rhodes floats freely, and the drums follow suit in an exercise that is as playful as it is anarchic. Here, the Mellotron reigns supreme alongside the distorted bass, representing the "rock 'n' roll" side of Guapo's avant-garde jazz-rock, while the music vibrates and sways, accelerating to perfectly complement what stands as the flip side of Five Suns. It wouldn't be complete without the other side of the coin, "Topan", where they deconstruct fusion in the style of Eskaton, with their degraded harmonies, only to end with the same mystery with which we began: an open-ended conclusion that serves as the best guarantee of an imminent return.
items._cn_summary: 这是一张以三重奏编制为核心的前卫专辑，吉他、采样器与鼓机在三位乐手间不断切换角色，制造出难以预测的声响景观。五段式套曲结构层层推进，从手风琴与钢琴的古典语汇出发，逐步引入Mellotron、风琴与失真吉他，在King Crimson式的不协和爵士摇滚与Mahavishnu式融合之间反复切换。评论特别强调乐队对节奏断裂时机的精准掌控——重复段落总在恰当时刻被打散，混沌与秩序的边界如同爵士即兴般始终被驾驭。第五部分以风琴独奏坠入深渊，而附加曲目'Mictlan'则展现出轻盈与流动的一面，Mellotron与失真贝斯并肩而立，释放出摇滚式的张力。整体而言，这张作品在密度、黑暗感与结构张力之间取得了平衡，是前卫摇滚向实验领域延伸的典型范例。

items.body:
This column is a loose gathering of recordings – two duos, two quartets – that might define a certain frontier, a degree of meaning in improvised interactivity spreading over 12 years. At times, the combination of close listening and simultaneous writing (the only way I can find to describe this music) results in verbal collisions that may be elusive in meaning, but they may also legitimately represent some of the transformative complexity and overlapping visions arising in these works of essentially collective invention. Though one of these recordings is more than a decade old, they may represent a kind of perpetual edge.

Certain musics can pass through walls of custom, identity, and meaning, assuming unknown shapes, escaping any strict verbal denotation, meaning becoming at once plastic and ineffable. Such music cannot be analyzed or described successfully, such failed exercises, however, perhaps contributing to both its mystery and its beauty, music that might suggest a hymn from an unknown culture, possibly disappeared, to an unknown deity, possibly deceased. In collectively improvised music, the role of the listener is paramount: assembling, collecting, composing ... At the same time, however, no interpretation is more privileged than another. These particular recordings are by musicians who can create dreams in sound. Some will imagine mills or factory floors, tuned to and amplifying unimaginable inventions of human industry. Empathy contributes a mutating, transformational soundscape. These are musics that create uncommon space.

Die Dritte Ebene (45 rpm LP, NiVuNiConnu, nvnc-lp062) by Emilio Gordoa and the late Sven-Åke Johansson might initially seem exotic. Ultimately, it’s not. It’s work of perfect transparency, that is, a view of whatever one hears as the other side of anywhere. The cover offers two titles, DIE DRITTE EBEN or EL TERCER NIVEL, “the third level,” in German or Spanish, with each phrase written with the “E”s written as reversed 3s. The phrase arises in Gordoa’s brief description appended to the Bandcamp page: “We were discussing how our music moves as if in parallel lines, and how after a while something third will emerge from it, almost like a ghost. It is something I find almost mystical: how this third level manifested itself in our playing without us thinking about it.”

Reminiscent of Johansson’s previous NiVuNiConnu release, Tea Time, with Nicholas Bussmann and Yan Jun, the music hints at Erik Satie’s Furniture Music, somehow constituting a radical background music that enhances consciousness, the special resonance of repeated materials creating a trance-like, near-ecstatic state, a reflective consciousness that rises between the parts created by Johansson and Gordoa, illuminating as well as hypnotic. Die Dritte Ebene, from August 26, 2023, points to an ineffable quality – a kind of trance, a kind of lift, a spectral point of attention that is produced in a listener’s collaboration with the close echoes, tight resonance and metallic rattle of Johansson’s snare, the reeds of his accordion, and the glassy ring of Gordoa’s vibraphone, glowing like light in sonic form. The shared insistence and simultaneity of Johansson and Gordoa’s work consistently expands what is essentially a minimalist musical environment, concluding with a strange abstraction of accordion and vibraphone that might suggest a kind of musical haunting.

Nate Wooley and Seymour Wright recorded About Trumpet and Saxophone in 2012, appearing on the Fataka label in 2013. While that release was unquestionably radical, its forthcoming successor, recorded in 2025, About Saxophone and Trumpet (Relative Pitch) takes a very different initial tack, opening with a deconstruction of the romantic ballad “The Midnight Sun,” composed by Lionel Hampton and Sonny Burke in 1947, recorded initially as an instrumental, with sufficient melodic grace to have lyrics later added by Johnny Mercer, spurring recordings by June Christy, Ella Fitzgerald, and Carmen McRae. Here the melody is clearly audible through a series of gasps, honks, and shattered, incomplete phrases, a nod to tradition that rapidly expands, becoming increasingly inclusive.

There follows “Experiment Four,” an extended dialogue which includes some of the strangest sounds ever emitted by saxophone and trumpet, often coming from very different positions in the sound spectrum. The fourth track, “Untitled,” is genuinely conversational, though the conversation is conducted in assorted bleats and blasts. Each musician is repeatedly triggered by the other’s material, whether pinching their sound inward, or adapting a radical extroversion. Music here will stand in for complex human relationships and perceptions, a sound store evolving to mark the impact of events in one’s daily life, worlds for which artists have long been refining their techniques and perceptions. As our descriptive apparatus daily fails before global events, our key artists stretch the elements. In that sense, call it modern syntactical practice or a soundtrack to Guernica, but the expressive range in which Wooley and Wright here operate seems perfectly in keeping with the daily news. Meanwhile, the inner tunings and sustained tones, even their matching fast vibratos suggest the development and synergy of an expressionist language. Sudden shifts will swiftly resemble elegant balladry of yore, echoes of that “Midnight Sun.”

While the Wooley/Wright duet recalls Fataka, Trevor Brent’s remarkable label – “‘dedicated to releasing recordings of small group and solo improvisations with a particular interest in situations where a common musical language has not yet fully emerged” – has become active again, releasing Parallels & Diagonals by a quartet from the label’s earlier period, 14th July 2014 at Cafe Oto, in which Wooley and Wright appear in a quartet with two percussionists active since the dawn of English free improvisation, Paul Lytton and Eddie Prévost. Contrary to Brent’s explanation of the label (and a genuine generational difference: the percussionists had discographies before the wind players were born), the four musicians seem so closely attuned – each a genuine spontaneous composer – that they sound like they might have had a long history together. Parallels and Diagonals is 12-year-old music, but it sounds like it might be recorded next year.

The opening track, the extended Parallel A, sounds like a machine shop that has discovered free improvisation, shifting dramatically after a passage of silence shortly after the 15-minute mark. The sounds suggest a light roll on a kettle drum, a brush on a cymbal, the sound of air pushed delicately through a trumpet. This notion of interiority marks the collective passage of these musicians, finding a terrain at once both barely imagined and yet a defining part of the human condition. In Diagonal A, fundamental gestures, like air squeezed through a metal tube, take on their own significance, behaving like Buddhist mudras, invoking fundamental gestures and symptoms of human life, murmurs, signs, abrasions. Diagonal B’s rapid actions and continuous overlapping suggest activity so closely attended by the musicians that it might follow a score in which the pauses might be carefully accounted, floating among a delicately bowed cymbal, other sounds that cannot be identified, and some that shimmer around audibility.

foam and mesh (Fundacja Słuchaj Records) by the B:A:N:S BAND is the work of pianist Sophie Agnel, saxophonist John Butcher, bassist Pascal Niggenkemper, and percussionist Ståle Liavik Solberg, recorded at the 2024 ArtAct Festival in St. Johann, Austria. While it’s the only grouping here with a conventional instrumental grouping, the orientation of the musicians will ensure that there is nothing resembling convention in the ways that the instruments are utilized.

foam and mesh I is clearly the main event, a 35-minute dialogue in which four of the most skilled spontaneous composers put together a dense weave of sonic events, with nothing predictable, yet everything interlocking. Tension curves are developed with astonishing power, each member of the quartet seemingly pursuing a unique and independent path, yet everything contributing to an astonishing rhythmic taffy-pull in which every part contribute to a compound and original overall momentum. This complex relationship will sustain through numerous group movements, whether slow balladic ruminations with isolated knocks and flurries or a sudden tense wedding of trembling oscillations, all four musicians regularly finding distinct timbres. The relatively brief foam and mesh II initially foregrounds Agnel’s piano, her focus initially on brief, isolated, tight-knit clusters with abstract flurries from Niggenkemper’s bass and the randomizing knitwork of Liavik Solberg. When Butcher initially enters on soprano saxophone, the random patterns generally coalesce into a continuous stream of different rhythms and complementary densities before the work’s ultimately gradual disappearance.

items.body:
Gerry Hemingway leads a band of globe-trotters: German multi-reedist Frank Gratkowski whose recorded in the US often; pianist Izumi Kimura based in Ireland; Swiss bassist Christian Weber who’s recorded on three continents, crossing paths along the way with Yanks Oliver Lake, Ellery Eskelin, Nate Wooley, and Russ Johnson; Gerry himself, based in Lucerne since 2009.

In many ways Hemingway’s contemporary music mines his time in Anthony Braxton’s wondrous 1985-1993 quartet. The leaping staccato melody with asymmetrical phrases near the top of the 36-minute “Bau 4 Assembly” is one marker; another, the way that loose suite and the 23-minute “Slivers” use long improvised sections to tie together occasional scored episodes – not that Braxton was alone in that. And Braxton’s quartet prompted Hemingway’s duo with bandmate Marilyn Crispell, prefiguring his duo with Kimura in recent years.

On the CD, a six-minute Hemingway-Kimura improvisation is sandwiched between the long pieces, but I tend to cue up that “Third Story Variation” first, for its unbeatable interplay. The pianist and drummer catch and ride the same pulse, leaving plenty of air but also knowing how to fill various spaces along the way. Their timbral senses are fully compatible: her under-the-hood preparations tilt her sound drumward. They’ll set up a slow groove together, then she’ll use her other hand to play against it. It’s all very attentive and effective.

The longer pieces credited to Hemingway unfold like narratives, with discreet episodes, varied pacing, subgroup subplots, ways to build and dispel tension. “Slivers” is for trio, minus piano, Gratkowski leading off on squawky bass clarinet, tracked by Weber’s bass; the time feel is notably looser than the duo’s. A few minutes in, bass clarinet exits, and Frank’s re-entrance on disembodied wispy alto is placed just right: an instant orchestrator’s decision. Later there’s a section for low bass clarinet and arco bass in frictive unison under free drum rustle – suggesting Braxton’s love of the sub-basement, and the flexible trio dynamic of Gerry’s early/longtime vehicle BassDrumBone. But “Slivers” does slack off a bit between the scored tentpoles. There are times you wish the drummer would apply a firmer hand in a what-would-Billy-Higgins-do kind of way. One of Gerry’s signatures at the traps is a free-swinging–arms sense of relaxation, hitting the skins as if on the rebound, with some hits maybe dropped or delayed in transit. In the closing minutes, and on the closing theme, he can come off like someone who thinks he’s swinging harder than he is.

All four assemble for “Bau 4 Assembly” which makes up the bulk of the program. The venue Bau 4 in Altbüron, Switzerland was founded by folks in the timber business, and is located in their commercial compound. In tribute, Gerry and company play or use as beaters wood scraps retrieved from the workshop, notably heard around 10 minutes in, on a fast irregular clacky and texturally light colloquy which develops into something like pointillism with a groove (no small achievement) before flute and pedal-down piano soften things up. But not for long; in very short order, a scrapwood and piano gamelan. Midway, there’s a long-tone chapter with clarinet, and Gerry singing wavery lines into his cymbals or (says here) through metal objects, an odd effect he just about pulls off. (There’s a little Robert Wyatt in his vocal wah-wahs.) The composer and the quartet cover much ground. Elsewhere, a slow line’s melodic contours are subtly mirrored by the drums.

We won’t catalog every change-up or chapter, but near the end there’s a free-jazz blowout whose presence feels like checking a box – which is not to overlook Frank’s rapid multiphonic growls. (He’s got a great command of altissimo and pressurized reed textures.) Then they break into a loose brisk tempo, to frame that free-jazz energy. It arrives just where a non-drummer’s band would place a climactic the drum solo. Then a feint toward the Braxtonian head from half an hour earlier. A few staccato hits end things without a big fuss.

items._cn_summary: 这张现场专辑汇集了一支跨国籍乐队：德国多管乐演奏家Frank Gratkowski、爱尔兰钢琴手Izumi Kimura、瑞士贝斯手Christian Weber与定居琉森的鼓手Gerry Hemingway。Hemingway的创作深受其在Anthony Braxton四重奏（1985-1993）时期的影响，擅长以结构化段落串联长段即兴，形成松散的组曲形态。钢琴与鼓的二重奏《Third Story Variation》以极度敏锐的呼应著称，Kimura利用钢琴内部预置技法将音色推向鼓感，与Hemingway形成呼吸同步的律动关系。三重奏《Slivers》由低音单簧管与贝斯开场，展现BassDrumBone式的低音域张力。主打曲目《Bau 4 Assembly》长达36分钟，致敬瑞士木材厂场地Bau 4，乐队甚至使用从工坊回收的木块作为敲击工具，在第十分钟前后形成独特的木质敲击质感。整体编排讲究叙事性、组员分工与张力调度，是当代自由爵士与即兴音乐领域中结构感与开放性兼具的现场录音。

items.body: Palagoma is not only the first release from Nairobi-based label Cool Waters, it also marks the first time German-born, Kenya-based percussionist Sven Kacirek has collaborated with Ogoya Nengo and Olith Ratengo at the same time. Odd Okoddo, the duo of Kacirek and Ratengo, has been performing since 2018, but with the inclusion of the 83 year old Nengo, a singer from the eastern part of the country, there�s an added traditional depth to the music. A 2025 performance shows Nengo�s lifetime of experience singing Kenya�s dodo tradition around 2 and half minutes in (see below). Furthermore, her inclusion on this album allows her and Ratengo to toss the vocals back and forth as they reference their shared roots (Ratengo and Nengo live minutes from each other). Musically, however, the tracks are driven by Kacirek�s Buchla synth, hand percussion, and occasional kit drumming, which serve to buoy the voices without blotting out the music�s origins. Palagoma by Odd Okoddo & Ogoya Nengo �Bara,� for example, begins with the dime-store thwack of a repeated pattern, a stiff juxtaposition to the voices; yet, as the song rolls along, a 4/4 clink appears, then a burbling bass, and finally, what sounds like a xylophone. Layers of synthesized polyrhythms keep presenting themselves with a subtlety almost unnoticeable, until, by the track�s end, it feels organic, as if it�s all been underneath the two voices all along. Palagoma by Odd Okoddo & Ogoya Nengo �Sarah,� perhaps the album�s most intense track, features a lead vocal from Ratengo and tentative, percussive spittles from Kacirek. And while the technology never tries to overtake the vocals, it does sneak up and punctuate the track�s urgency, as edgy distortion sneaks in here and there just as Ratengo�s voice reaches its peak. The term �folktronica� has been bandied about as a way to house the type of music on offer here. In fact, exploratory collaborations such as Chouk Bwa & The �ngstr�mers as well as much of Kampala, Uganda�s Nyege Nyege label house sounds that might be �folktronic� in some way. What�s more interesting and important about this music, though, is how truly global so much of it is while maintaining a deep connection to Africa and its diasporic communities. The music on Palagoma , as well as much of what�s linked above (and available in countless other recent recordings) demonstrates a real willingness for cultures to respond to each other without trampling traditions altogether. Instead, roots become avant-garde and innovations become seemingly thousands of years old. Certainly the inclusion of an 83 year old traditional Kenyan singer only recently making her global debut as she tours with a duo whose instrumental voice is a white male saturated in electronic Kenyan rhythms demonstrates this blurring. The music this trio makes is certainly of the 21st century, but it�s often hazy, sparse, and open, keeping it from a quick sell-by date or confining it to a specific genre. Instead, it�s a beautiful example music as grace.

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑是内罗毕新厂牌Cool Waters的首发作品，核心是德国出生、扎根肯尼亚的打击乐手Sven Kacirek与Olith Ratengo组成的二人组Odd Okoddo，再邀请83岁的肯尼亚东部传统dodo歌唱家Ogoya Nengo共同录制。Kacirek以Buchla合成器、手打打击乐和架子鼓构建节奏底层，与两位歌手的人声交织。合成化的复合节奏以极隐晦的方式层层叠加，最终与声线融为一体，形成有机整体。Nengo与Ratengo因地理邻近而共享传统根基，人声之间的呼应承载了代际传递的意味。整张专辑体现了当代全球音乐场景中的一种趋势：不同文化在不对抗传统的前提下彼此对话，电子手段与非洲根源音乐深度融合，呈现出既前卫又古老的听觉面貌。

items.album: Francesco Paolo Paladino and Luca Chino Ferrari
items.artist: Dorothy Moskowitz & United States of Alchemy
items.excerpt:
Known for playing with County Joe McDonald, and for her experimental sound band The United States of America, Dorothy Moskowitz came back in 2023 with United States of Alchemy and their well-received release,
Under an Endless Sky
.
In collaboration with avant-garde composer and filmmaker Francesco Paolo Paladino, and poet and music writer Luca Chino Ferrari,
Songs of Compassion
is eleven songs containing subversive and at times beautiful music, and richly evocative lyrics.
Francesco Paolo Paladi
items.body: Known for playing with County Joe McDonald, and for her experimental sound band The United States of America, Dorothy Moskowitz came back in 2023 with United States of Alchemy and their well-received release, Under an Endless Sky . In collaboration with avant-garde composer and filmmaker Francesco Paolo Paladino, and poet and music writer Luca Chino Ferrari, Songs of Compassion is eleven songs containing subversive and at times beautiful music, and richly evocative lyrics. Francesco Paolo Paladino and Luca Chino Ferrari | Photo by Maria Assunta Karini Songs of Compassion has two challenges for the listener. The first is the music, called variously avant-garde, ambient, modal, non-linear, and a few more. It is played mostly on pianos mixed in and out of the foreground, sometimes doubled, and sometimes out of phase, joined by strings, woodwinds, synth washes, and steely sounds. Initially disorienting, the music serves to remind us how locked our minds are to Western notions of harmonic movement. It speaks of alternative musical narratives much older and much further away. They are songs that subvert the song: more like Steve Reich than Steve Stills; more like Phillip Glass than Phil Collins. UNITED STATES OF ALCHEMY - Pale Wanderer At the same time, there are the poetic yet strikingly contemporary lyrics. �Pale Wanderer� talks about the fact that authoritarianism needs willing accomplices, describing what happens �When you make a deal with darkness.� UNITED STATES OF ALCHEMY (Dorothy Moskowitz, Francesco Paolo Paladino e Luka Chino Ferrari) by Silentes �Charlottesville� (written with the late Joe Byrd) evokes the time not long ago when torch-wielding nazis, proud of the metaphoric Ns on their tunics, chanted the antisemitic tropes paraphrased in Moskowitz�s words, �We�ll be one people, pure of race/No greedy throng could take our place� . Besides the overtly political lyrics, in the tradition of 1960s protest songs, there are also thoughtful meditations on mortality and our place in the universe. The message is high-minded yet sincere and direct. World weary and wise, Moskowitz�s voice inhabits the evocative philosophical lyrics with the authority of a skilled method actor. The melodies unfold like streams of consciousness, rising and falling, not following expected diatonic chord progressions, but honouring, instead, the value of each word. Moskowitz�s piano acts as another voice and sometimes a kind of Greek chorus commenting on the proceedings. The surrounding music frames, creates pulses and dissonances, and shimmers. The return of Dorothy Moskowitz with her renamed project has arrived in a moment quite similar to the times that spawned its predecessor. Political division, unrest, and uncertainty always generate artistic reaction, and United States of Alchemy roared back to life with their epic 24-minute opening track �Under an Endless Sky� in 2023, serving perhaps as an �In-A-Gadda-Da-Vida� for our times. Songs of Compassion continues to challenge how we think about our world. It�s music that defies the song form, while doing exactly what music is supposed to do�enrich the human condition. items._cn_summary: Dorothy Moskowitz 携改名后的 United States of Alchemy 回归，与作曲家 Francesco Paolo Paladino 及诗人 Luca Chino Ferrari 合作推出专辑《Songs of Compassion》，收录十一首作品。音乐以钢琴为核心，辅以弦乐、木管、合成器泛音与金属质感声响，刻意脱离西方和声运动惯例，采用非线性的调式与相位错位手法，将极简主义的循环结构与电影化的氛围铺陈融合，既不像传统歌曲，也不像纯器乐。歌词兼具诗意与政治性，从《Pale Wanderer》对极权主义的隐喻，到与已故 Joe Byrd 合作的《Charlottesville》直指新纳粹集会，语言延续六十年代抗议歌曲传统同时具有当代现实关怀。Moskowitz 的演唱如同方法派演员般投入，钢琴充当另一声部与希腊合唱团般的评论角色，与环绕的环境声响共同构建沉思空间。整体呈现出实验性、沉思性与社会批判的融合。

items.body: A confession to begin: I�ve been a fan of Alison Cotton�s music for quite a while, so the announcement of a new album definitely brought me a frisson of delight. The Gods Laugh certainly doesn�t disappoint, with the same deliciously amorphous feel that�s defined her other work, drawing on folk, the avant-garde, as well as a sense of religiosity to make the music here, possibly best exemplified in �I Am!�, where she set a poem by John Clare, England�s great nature poet, to a transcendent melody over the constant underpinning of a lulling drone. While the playing revolves around her usual arsenal of viola, harmonium, hammered dulcimer, and piano, along with some percussion, on this album she also adds some drums, bass and synthesizer. The music is often improvised and captured in a single take, with an almost mystical, hushed sensibility that seems to reach through time, as with �I Still Know You are Calling My Name,� where the tune could have been plucked from an old folk song. Sprigs of Heather by Alison Cotton The centerpiece, however, is �Sprigs of Heather,� with an opening that recalls medieval sacred music that becomes a simple, slowly cascading, piano-led melody. It�s far from the longest track on the album, but a little pearl of perfection that carries the listener away. Sprigs of Heather by Alison Cotton The Gods Laugh is a memorial of sorts to Cotton�s father, who died in late 2024. There�s a sense of loss reaching across these tracks, most specifically present on �The Final Harvest,� a solemn piece about her father�s last visit to the allotment he loved so much. It�s suffused with tenderness that extends beyond words. Light and darkness bleed into each other across the music, and moods shift. It�s music that happily stands beyond category, with hints of so many things, but ultimately standing as Alison Cotton music, which might well be all the definition it needs. It will challenge you but also satisfy and move you. What more can you wish from music? Find the artist online.
