items.body: In August of this year, New Focus Recordings released New Music for Two Voices, an impressive collection of acapella vocal music by sopranos Susan Narucki and Kirsten Ashley Wiest. This lavish album features a full hour masterful singing of six contemporary works, including three world premiere recordings. Susan Narucki is an accomplished soprano who has appeared as a soloist with the Cleveland Orchestra, Los Angeles Philharmonic, the San Francisco Symphony, among many other international appearances. She is presently on the faculty of the Department of Music at UC San Diego. Kirsten Ashley Wiest is an award-winning coloratura soprano who has performed and recorded alongside numerous GRAMMY winners, the Los Angeles Philharmonic, San Diego Symphony, Bang on a Can All-Stars and the Partch ensemble, among many others. Kirsten currently teaches voice at San Bernardino Valley College and University of California Riverside, New Music for Two Voices is a deep dive into the cutting edge of virtuoso vocal technique as it intersects with contemporary musical composition. The album is accompanied by excellent liner notes, full translations of the texts and biographical notes on the composers and the performers. The outstanding sound engineering is by Andrew Munsey and Kristina Tran. The first track on the album is come sempre (2025), by Dutch composer Rozalie Hirs. Although written just last year, the liner notes inform that this piece “…evokes music of an earlier time, with shifting tonal centers and interwoven melodic lines..” Running at over 7 minutes, it is one of the longer works of the entire album and is a world premiere. come sempre features two voices singing separately in Italian, sometimes together and sometimes in a call and response pattern. The vocal lines are often independent and weave in and around each other seamlessly in a series of lovely harmonies. There is no accompaniment anywhere in this album so the two singers must rely on their internal sense of rhythm and pitch. Where crisp phrases are present, these are always clean and punchy. Nothing ragged or blurry here; the notes are precise and balanced. As the piece proceeds it gradually increases in complexity, summoning ever greater technique. The singing by these two confident voices, however, is always controlled throughout. The poems of El trino persistente by Javier Tafur González are the inspiration for TRINOS, a series of twelve miniature works by Colombian composer Alba Potes. Commissioned by Susan Narucki in 2024, all are less than one minute long, yet these pieces sparkle like brilliant gems. The liner notes state that “Each of the twelve settings seems to capture a moment in time—by turns, lyrical, nostalgic, jubilant, hopeful.” “TRINOS: I. Jazmin” is the first of the twelve pieces and although less than a minute in length, it sets the standard for the precision and vocal technique that is heard throughout the entire work. A high vocal tone opens, then falls rapidly in pitch as a second voice joins in a middle register with dissonance. The singers must rely on their own intuition for pitch and timing – there are no accompanying chords or common rhythms. The overall feeling is one of welcome and portent. Although less than a minute in length, this first piece sets a high bar for vocal artistry. Other pieces in the work are similarly concise and illustrate the consistent level of virtuosity brought to bear by Wiest and Narucki. “TRINOS: II. Entra illuminando la casa”, at just 32 seconds in length ,is intense, with many jumps and leaps in the two voices. It shines like a fiery jewel. “TRINOS: IV. No saldré” features a middle register voice together with a lower voice in close harmony. Stretches of unusual dissonances challenge the singers, but are navigated successfully. “TRINOS: VI. Timida flor” opens with a strong voice soaring up very high with impressive power and good control. “TRINOS: VII. Ven, anclemos” is soft, with almost mournful feeling and quietly sentimental. The text, even in English translation, is perfect: “Come, let us anchor now hands entwined.” “TRINOS: IX. Se hundió el buque” by contrast, is completely different. A quiet, solo voice is heard in a middle register, reserved and subdued. The lyrics are more spoken than sung, producing a purposeful and deliberate sensibility. “TRINOS: XI. Podemos estar juntos” is another solo piece with a strong voice crying out as if in sadness. The singing here is expressive, yet delivered with great clarity. The final piece in the work is “TRINOS: XII. En los hilos”, a duet with the lower voice in sustained tones underneath a soaring, coloratura voice. The dissonances in the harmonies add a powerful, melancholy feeling to this. TRINOS is a masterful collection of small pieces that each deliver an emotional punch from the virtuosity of the performers. The third work on the album is From the Grammar of Dreams (1988), by Kaija Saariaho and consists of five pieces based on two separate texts from the American poet Sylvia Plath. The liner notes tell us that “The five duets demonstrate Saariaho’s unique compositional language, with its attention to fine gradations of vocal color, intricacy and flexibility of gesture, and a nearly overwhelming range of emotional expression.” The first duet, labeled simply “I”, opens with strange and painful sounds in the lower voice with struggling vocals in the second voice as if forcing out the words and notes. Leaps and jumps are heard in the upper voice accompanied by sustained and plaintive sounds from the lower. Just a little over 2 minutes long, this piece is expressively weird and haunting.“II”, the second piece in From the Grammar of Dreams begins with two sets of spoken words heard simultaneously. This is somewhat chaotic as there is no common tones or phrasing. One voice includes some rather gruesome details, as if recounting a nightmare. The voices are alternately speaking and singing and often very agitated. The music is complex and dynamic, yet confidently delivered. The third duet, “III” is soft and melodic; completely different in character from the previous pieces. There is lovely harmony in the two voices with lots of sustained notes and dramatic gestures. There is a welcome and mysterious feeling to this. “IV” opens with scratchy, breathy sounds followed by strong vocal music. The voices jump and soar as each part bounces breathlessly off the other. The two voices devolve in a sort of shouting match just before the piece concludes with a few short breaths. Amazing technique here. The final duet, “V”, begins with a series of sustained notes in both voices sung in a high register with prominent vibrato. The sounds loop around each other independently in pitch and dynamic. This produces an eerie feeling at times but is mostly strongly declarative. The fourth work on the album is NauðaR Níu [The Nine Needs] (2025), by Jeffrey Holmes. This collection of nine pieces is based on old Norse Runic carvings (ca. 5th through 12th century), as compiled and translated by the composer. As with the other works in this album, each piece is short, ranging from 37 seconds to a little over three and a half minutes. As explained in the liner notes, NauðaR Níu features some unusual accompaniment: “Throughout, the vocalists play a variety of percussion instruments; the sound of metal, skin, wood and natural materials contributing to the sense of a vast primeval landscape.” The opening piece of NauðaR Níu, titled simply “I”, starts with soft tones by two voices. As this one minute piece proceeds, a gentle gong sound and some light percussion are heard; a subtle and mysterious beginning. “II” sets a completely different tone. A sharp drum rap begins, serving as a starting exclamation point. The two voices weave in and around each other in sustained tones amid much howling and spooky vocals. Another series of bangs from the drum and a woodblock add to the unnerving atmosphere. “III” returns to a more settled and soothing feeling. A low sustained vocal in one voice is made more expressive by the light tinkling of chimes. Very mystical and solemn with lovely vocals and reverential sentiment. “IV” continues in a sacred feeling, opening with an Ahhh sound in a single voice. Another voice joins in, accompanied by quiet gong tones and a low drone. The exotic – almost Asian – feel of this is supported by devout vocals, gentle chimes and percussion. “V” continues in the exotic groove and returns to the more forward style with drum raps and sharp woodblock beats. The voices seeming to chant with out words but in eerie, sustained tones. There is a decidedly spectral and anxious feeling to this. “VI” returns to the more subdued refinement heard in “IV”, with a soft opening and chimes. A sudden drum strike with wood block recalls the mood in “II”. A gong is heard between the sustained and almost mournful vocals. There is a sacred, worshipful feel to this. “VII” continues with chimes and a high, plaintive opening vocal. The top voice soars in very high, airy sweeps. More chimes accompany. The excellent singing, heard in very high registers, is controlled, on pitch and does not lose its power. “VIII” opens with a strong drum strike and woodblock rap. Loud, almost screaming vocals are heard, as if in great surprise. A palpable sense of danger and fear is present. Loud drum and woodblock strikes accompanied by long, descending sweeps of vocals paint a convincing musical portrait of fear and despair, This sets the stage for the final section, “IX” which opens with a haunting vocal solo , soon joined by the second voice in call and response. The voices are subdued with somber descending pitches and accompanied by drum strikes, chimes and gong strikes. All elements of the various sections seemingly combine into a sense of acceptance and fateful resignation. Beautiful, expressive singing is heard as the vocals fade to the finish. With NauðaR Níu, Jeffrey Holmes has forged a vibrant musical connection between the Old Norse culture and our own.The next work on the album is a collection of five short pieces titled Two Walking (1994) by French composer Pascal Dusapin. The text for Two Walking is by American writer Gertrude Stein and the work was originally conceived by Dusapin as a study for his chamber opera To Be Sung. The opening piece of Dusapin’s collection, titled “I. How many little wings” begins with a single lyrical voice followed closely be a second vocal, almost as an echo. Now the higher voice soars in a sustained upward arc with text following in both voices. The vocals bounce and dance around each other, evoking birdlike acrobatics on the wing. As the tempo increases the text becomes louder and more frenetic. A sudden slowing towards the finish provides the listener with a soft landing. “ II. Kiss my lips” begins with a quiet clicking and two voices in a sort of conversation. There is a whispering and intimate feel to this, sung as if in secret. “III. May, June” opens with a long solo note followed by the second voice entering slightly below in a counter melody. Now the notes in each voice volley back and forth effectively. As the text moves faster, crisply sung in short, quick phrases, the result is a pleasingly complex texture that does not sacrifice the beautiful harmonies. “IV. A scene in singing” has both voices starting together but soon singing separate lines. Short snappy phrases are heard in places and at times the harmony is unusual, but the overall effect is both lovely and abstract. The final piece in the Dusapin work is “ V. It seems to be”. Two voices in lower register open in syncopated rhythms and the separate vocal lines produce an engaging, crunchy texture. The pitches and harmony are controlled and balanced, even with the lively phrasing. “ V. It seems to be” is a fine finish to an intriguing work. The concluding work on the album is Melisande (2022), by Marti Epstein, the longest piece at almost 13 minutes. Inspired by the Debussy opera, Epstein re-imagines the story as if told through Melisande’s own experience, rather than as a reflection of others. In this interpretation, “the two sopranos alternate between extending and finishing each other’s words, functioning as a single unit, or singing passages with overlapping, contrapuntal lines that give way to moments of ecstatic release.” Melisande opens with two sustained voices in a delicate harmony and dynamics that vary intriguingly. The vocals become more active, with independent lines weaving in and around each other in a call and response pattern. By 4:10 the voices are singing in common phrases in an effective contrast to the opening. The upper voice is especially impressive, exhibiting a fine tone with strength and confidence. By 7:10 the vocals are in solid harmony and declarative text sung expressively in middle registers. The lines diverge and become occasionally independent, one often following the other. The duet singing here is especially disciplined and precise. At a slowing of the tempo, Melisande fades quietly to its finish. An excellent performance of technically challenging music.New Music for Two Voices is a dazzling exploration of vocal virtuosity that sets – and meets – a very high standard. Hopefully this premiere album by Susan Narucki and Kirsten Ashley Wiest will be the first of more to follow. New Music for Two Voices is available in digital download or CD format from: Bandcamp:HB Direct: The post Susan Narucki & Kirsten Ashley Wiest – New Music for Two Voices appeared first on Sequenza21.

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑由两位女高音演绎六首当代无伴奏声乐作品，其中三首为世界首录。曲目涉及荷兰作曲家Rozalie Hirs的come sempre（2025），以意大利语双声部交织，展现对早期音乐语汇的引用与扩展；哥伦比亚作曲家Alba Potes的TRINOS由十二首不到一分钟的微型作品组成，基于诗人Tafur González的文本，每段捕捉不同的瞬间情绪。整张专辑无任何伴奏，完全依靠歌手对节奏与音高的内在把控，双声部在卡农式呼应与独立线条间无缝切换，和声层次清晰且精准，技术难度递增但始终保持控制力。录音由Andrew Munsey和Kristina Tran担纲，配以详尽的解说词、全文本翻译及作曲家和演奏者传记。作为新音乐厂牌New Focus Recordings的发行的确在当代声乐写作的前沿地带进行了一次深入探索。

items.body: Review by arcane-beautiful — Solaris by The Ocean is a great step forward for the German sludgy atmospheric prog metallers, allowing new vocalists Enrico Tiberi & Lane Shi great room to show off their unique talents. Musically more epic since their Phanerozoic album series, it sees the band create longer compositions that gives great drama and atmosphere. While I was a massive fan of former vocalist L�ic Rossetti, Tiberi's cleans and barks are a perfect replacement, adding the same drama and emotion but with his own unique flair, while Shi's unique chants and screams are an extra dimension to the bands sound, which adds an almost creepy mood to the thick atmosphere the band create. The use of industrial electronic noises throughout are also great at adding mood to the overall pieces. I'd give this a mid 8 out of 10. The track I'd recommend is Belligerence.
items._cn_summary: 德国乐队 The Ocean 在这张专辑中拓展了此前化石系列以来的史诗化倾向，作品以更长的篇幅铺陈戏剧性与氛围层次。新主唱 Enrico Tiberi 兼具清声与嘶吼，延续前任 Loïc Rossetti 的情感张力，同时加入 Lane Shi 的吟唱与尖叫，为整体厚重的音墙增添近乎诡异的阴郁色彩。工业电子噪音作为贯穿全作的氛围手法，强化了器乐段落的情绪渲染。乐评整体持肯定态度，给予中段 8 分推荐，并特别指出 Belligerence 为首选曲目。该作在重金属框架内融入工业与实验元素，与用户关注的暗潮、工业及实验音乐偏好形成部分交集。

items.body: There was a useful logic to the running order of Friday night’s show at Klub Łącznik. Antibody, Agonoize and System Noire all make music designed to work physically, but they approach that physicality from quite different directions. Antibody built movement through rhythm and the almost compulsive momentum of hard electronic dance music. Agonoize converted it into confrontation, theatrical violence and direct exchange between performer and crowd. System Noire then expanded the same basic principle into something broader and increasingly combustible, combining electronic force with the dynamics of a full band. The evening became an accumulation of different ways of controlling a room. The concert was part of the 2026 run pairing Agonoize with System Noire, with Antibody as special guest; for System Noire, the tour also marks the Hanover band’s 10th anniversary. The Wrocław date was officially scheduled at Klub Łącznik, the concert space within Czasoprzestrzeń at the former Dąbie tram depot. Antibody Photos: Karo Kratochwil Antibody opened the evening, and first a small correction worth making because the name is easily mangled: the project is the work of Jan Laustroer. Laustroer began Antibody in 2013, when he was only twelve, and over the following years developed a sound drawing on industrial, power noise, dark electro and the harder end of rave and hardcore. The debut album Opera of Death appeared in 2017, while the more recent Never Quite Right was released in 2024. In January this year Antibody also collaborated with Grendel on “The Ranidae.” What worked especially well in Wrocław was that none of this required the opening slot to pretend it was already the climax of the night. Antibody’s set was extremely danceable, rhythmically insistent and immediately mobile. The tracks worked through repetition, sharp changes of pressure and bass strong enough to make the body respond before there was much reason to analyse what was happening. It was energetic without becoming shapeless; Jan understands that hard electronic music needs more than volume and speed if it is supposed to sustain movement. The visual presentation supported that. Against a star-filled background, the recurring frogs added a deliberately absurd signature to a set otherwise built around hard, mechanical momentum. They have become an immediately recognisable part of Antibody’s visual vocabulary, and after this year’s Grendel collaboration The Ranidae, their presence felt even more appropriate. There was something rather charming about the collision: pounding industrial rhythm underneath, a small amphibian mythology unfolding behind it. As an opener, Antibody did exactly what was needed. The set did not simply “warm up” the audience in the conventional sense; it established movement as the evening’s basic mode of communication. By the time it ended, the room was no longer waiting for the main acts. Agonoize Photos: Karo Kratochwil The change was immediately visible when Agonoize came on. The space in front of the stage became noticeably denser, bodies moved closer together, and the kind of dancing established during Antibody’s set turned into something more collective and more aggressive. Agonoize were formed in Berlin in 2002 and have spent more than two decades making the relationship between harsh electronic music and extreme stage performance central to their identity. Their current touring page explicitly designated the Wrocław concert as a “Blutshow”, continuing the use of theatrical blood that has long been part of the band’s live language. Their most recent full studio album remains Revelation Six Six Sick, released through RepoRecords in April 2021. Calling what happened at Łącznik simply “brutal” would miss why the set worked. The force was carefully organised. The electronics were dense, abrasive and extremely physical, but they also retained enough rhythmic definition for the material to still work as dance music. Chris L.’s performance depends heavily on this ambiguity: he confronts the audience while simultaneously demanding its participation. And participate they did. The stage blood is obviously theatrical, but the reaction it produces is real. Chris repeatedly showered the front of the audience with it, leaving faces and clothes streaked red, and the people closest to the stage seemed delighted to become part of the spectacle. The distinction is important. Agonoize’s blood show does not function particularly well when treated as something happening to a passive crowd. In Wrocław it became reciprocal. People moved forward knowing very well what was coming. They danced harder, reached towards the stage and quite visibly enjoyed being pulled inside the performance. That made the visual violence feel less like decoration attached to the songs and more like an extension of their physical logic. Chris’s gestures were large and confrontational because the music required a body capable of matching its exaggeration. The show continually crossed the line between concert and grotesque theatre without allowing the theatrical element to weaken the musical one. The encore shifted the visual vocabulary again. Chris returned wearing wings, and after so much aggression, blood and pressure, the image had a surprisingly different weight. It was beautiful precisely because the evening had not prepared us for beauty in any conventional form. The wings did not suddenly turn the performance sentimental; they introduced another register into a stage language that had spent most of the set emphasising impact and provocation. My conversation with Chris afterwards changed how I thought about the performance even further. We had previously discussed his long absence following a very serious illness, but hearing him describe the extent of the recovery in person gave that history a different scale. He spoke about having to rebuild abilities that most people never consciously think about, including basic everyday tasks and forms of recognition, through an exhausting rehabilitation process. I would not want to turn illness into an inspirational narrative imposed on the concert, because that would reduce both the person and the performance. But it does change the meaning of what one has just witnessed. Returning to a stage is one thing. Returning to this kind of stage presence, where the performance demands constant physical engagement, vocal force, timing, theatrical control and the ability to command a densely packed room, is something else. The striking thing was not simply that Chris was back. It was the absence of caution in the performance. In our recent interview, he told me that he has nothing to prove to anyone except himself and that what he wants, fundamentally, is simply to continue making music. Watching this set, that statement became much less abstract. The stamina was visible, certainly, but more important was the appetite behind it. This did not look like someone tentatively reclaiming an old position. It looked like someone fully inhabiting it again. System Noire Photos: Karo Kratochwil If Agonoize generated the evening’s most theatrical violence, System Noire converted the accumulated energy into something broader and, by the end, almost unruly. The Hanover project was founded in 2016 and is celebrating its tenth anniversary this year. Its current formation has grown beyond the original electronic core, and the band’s recent material increasingly allows guitars and a harder industrial-metal edge to interfere with its dark-electro and EBM foundations. Their 2024 album Aftermath includes ten tracks and was followed in February 2025 by Lost Control, whose single version the band themselves describe as harder and more guitar-driven, while a separate club edit strips it back towards electronics. That tension between programmed precision and a more volatile live-band attack was exactly what made the final set work. By this stage the audience no longer needed persuading. Smoke filled the stage, the lighting became much more aggressive, and the room that Antibody had initially taught to move and Agonoize had pushed into increasingly physical participation now had very little reserve left. System Noire used that. Their music has enough melodic architecture to keep the songs readable even when the performance becomes extremely dense. That mattered here. The combination of electronics, forceful vocals, percussion and the heavier edges of the current sound could easily have collapsed into undifferentiated volume; instead, the rhythmic centre remained very clear. People could dance to it. The lighting and smoke also worked unusually well with that construction. They were not merely there to make the stage appear “dark”. Smoke repeatedly altered what could actually be seen: musicians emerged, disappeared and reappeared as the lights cut through it, creating a visual equivalent of the music’s own alternation between defined melodic lines and heavier blocks of sound. And gradually the whole thing became wonderfully disorderly. By the final part of the set, the dancefloor was no longer behaving like a room of individuals politely occupying their allotted space. Movement propagated through it. People were dancing hard, responding to the band and to one another, and the distinction between observing the show and physically participating in it had largely disappeared. Calling it carnage is not much of an exaggeration, although it was an exceptionally friendly form of carnage. System Noire therefore made sense as the final band, even though Agonoize might initially appear the more obvious dramatic climax. Their set did not need to out-provoke what had come before it. Instead, it took the accumulated kinetic energy of the entire evening and gave it somewhere to go. Klub Łącznik Photos: Karo Kratochwil Klub Łącznik itself deserves some credit for why the evening felt so comfortable despite the intensity inside. The venue sits within Czasoprzestrzeń at the former Dąbie tram depot, and its layout provides something particularly useful for this kind of scene event: a clear separation between the physical density of the concert hall and the open area outside. Inside, there is a proper concrete-floored club space where a hard-electronic show can become as loud, smoky and physically crowded as it needs to be. Outside, the yard changes the social rhythm completely. Between sets people could step out, cool down, talk, meet friends and, importantly, encounter the musicians without the strange separation that larger venues often create between audience and performers. That mattered more than it might sound. A night involving three relentlessly physical electronic sets can become exhausting when there is nowhere for the intensity to dissipate. At Łącznik, it could. The outside conversations, pauses and meetings with the bands gave the evening breathing space, while every return indoors felt like deliberately re-entering the pressure. Three approaches, one increasingly crowded dancefloor What I liked most was that the evening had progression without needing an artificial concept imposed on it afterwards. Antibody made the body move through rhythmic precision and rave-derived momentum. Agonoize turned the same physical response into confrontation, participation and grotesque theatre. System Noire then took an audience already pushed far beyond passive listening and drove that energy through the dynamics of a full, forceful live set. The crowd grew thicker, sweatier and considerably bloodier as the night progressed, but the atmosphere never became hostile. Quite the opposite. There was a great deal of warmth underneath the noise: people dancing, talking outside, meeting musicians, returning inside and throwing themselves back into it. And perhaps that is the detail worth keeping. With music this aggressive, the obvious vocabulary is always brutality, darkness, violence and impact. All of those things were present. What made the Wrocław show successful, however, was how much pleasure there was inside that aggression. Antibody looked playful behind the pounding rhythms and wandering frogs. Agonoize turned theatrical bloodshed into something the front rows actively wanted to share. System Noire finished with smoke, light and enough accumulated movement to make the floor feel barely contained. By the end, Klub Łącznik looked appropriately wrecked, and the people inside it looked extremely happy. About Agonoize, System Noire and Antibody Agonoize formed in Berlin in 2002 around vocalist Chris L. and have built more than two decades of work around harsh electronic music paired with extreme, theatrically violent stage shows. Their most recent full studio album, “Revelation Six Six Sick,” was released through RepoRecords in April 2021; Side-Line marked that release with a streaming concert announcement at the time. Earlier releases include the 2019 EP “Blutgruppe Jesus (-) / Schmerzpervers 2.0” and the album “Midget Vampire Porn.” Ahead of the Wrocław date, Side-Line interviewed Chris L. about returning to the stage after a serious illness and new material. System Noire, from Hanover, were founded in 2016 and marked their tenth anniversary in 2026. Side-Line first profiled the project in a 2017 Face The Beat feature. The band’s sound has expanded from its original electronic base to include guitars and a heavier industrial-metal edge, documented on the 2024 album “Aftermath” and the February 2025 single “Lost Control.” Antibody is the project of Jan Laustroer, who began releasing music under the name in 2013 at the age of twelve. Side-Line introduced Antibody in a 2016 Face The Beat profile and later featured the track “Secrets” as a 2019 free download. Laustroer’s debut album, “Opera of Death,” followed in 2017, with “Never Quite Right” arriving in 2024. In January 2026, Antibody collaborated with Grendel on “The Ranidae.” Agonoize, System Noire and Antibody played Klub Łącznik, the concert venue inside the Czasoprzestrzeń cultural centre at Wrocław’s former Dąbie tram depot, on September 25, 2026.

items.body: 040118180514 and 102119200914. No, these aren't the result of my cat stepping on my keyboard; they're pseudonyms for the members of Endspace, an experimental black metal duet hailing from Canada, who have been constantly reinforcing their "sci-fi black metal" sound through a trail of releases leading up to their debut record—or "transmission", per the record's pattern of naming each song as a sequential broadcast. Whatever is contained within First Contact, it's going to be alien as hell. As predicted, First Contact is hypnotizingly strange. Dissonant metal genres are already on another plane of disorientation, but Endspace ramp the perplexity up tenfold, via the myriad synths, electronics, and vocoders at the duo's disposal, mostly implemented in their "singing". 040... and 120...'s vocals genuinely sound like extraterrestrial communications. After thirty-nine minutes however, the gimmick gets tiring. In fact, the second transmission alone exemplifies how overpowering their incomprehensible "vocals" can be. Across the nine transmissions, the "vocals" range from the pitch of a dog whistle to murky, gurgly depths, and once—during "Seventh Transmission"—can you pick up a robot warning the "system engaged." Everything, including that excerpt, is also always too loud for whatever mood First Contact is currently in, with zero instrumental tracks providing a much-desired break. "Ninth Transmission", is a particular offender, being constructed in a repeating calm/harsh pattern, and the recurring blasts have a high chance of blowing an eardrum or two.It sucks, because underneath the alien mess that are the vocals, Endspace play commendable dissonant and technical black metal. The streak from the "Seventh" to "Ninth" transmissions, plus the chug-centered niceness that is "Third Transmission", all feature guitar-forward, chaotic deliciousness, whose overhaul of electronics donates a symphonic feel to the record. This helps the otherworldly atmospheres, with the positively overpowering climax of "Fourth Transmission" providing the pinnacle of symphonics. Elsewhere, keyboard lines sound like opera notes and any synth undertone majorly assists any song it's found in. The tracks without a metal attitude, however, leave room for the aforementioned annoyances that are the vocals. The "Second", "Fifth", and "Sixth" transmissions are the definite weak spots in First Contact, with the fifth leaning too much into a noisy electronic beat.While the execution of First Contact was as experimental and wacky as I hoped it'd be, I bit off way more than I could chew with this LP. Tinny, vocoded emanations bury rather pleasing metal, resulting in a listen that I'm not anticipating returning to anytime soon, and doesn't further my desire for Endspace to make a second acquaintance. First Contact by ENDSPACE

items._cn_summary: Endspace 来自加拿大的二人组合，以"科幻黑金属"为定位，将黑金属的不和谐骨架与大量合成器、电子音效、人声合成器深度融合。九首曲目被命名为"传输"序列，营造出外星通讯般的概念氛围。器乐层面表现扎实，吉他主导的混乱段落兼具技术性与交响感，键盘与合成器铺垫构建出宏大的异世界空间感。然而人声处理贯穿始终，从高频啸叫到低频咕哝的电子变声在长达三十九分钟的篇幅中显得过度饱和，部分曲目因缺乏器乐间奏而失去呼吸空间。整体在实验性与可听性之间的平衡偏向前者，金属骨架被电子人声所遮蔽，对偏好极端实验的听众具有探索价值，但难以广泛复用。

items.body: John Coltrane – The John Coltrane Quartet Plays (Impulse, 1965) By Dan Sorrells Most of my listening hours are spent on freely improvised music. But when it comes to Coltrane, I love the classic quartet, 1965, right before things broke open (and the group, apart). The John Coltrane Quartet Plays is what I reach for most often. “Chim Chim Cheree” starts like another “My Favorite Things,” but less than a minute in, Coltrane’s already chafing against the melody, and after two he and Jones are fairly bursting out of Tyner’s measured vamp. “Brazilia” and “Nature Boy” enticingly point toward the searching explorations to come, where ideas were turned inside-out in dizzying, kaleidoscopic epics (something further evidenced by various surfaced recordings from the Half Note during the same period, where “Chim” and “Song of Praise” stretch to twice the length). The sense that traditional song forms must still be made to contain Trane’s increasingly frenetic probing lends indelible tension to the music; these songs are like swelling water ballons, but they’re filled with boiling water. For those of us in the future, it’s all the more heightened when you know just how far things will get pushed, even before the close of the year. Email This BlogThis! Share to X Share to Facebook
items._cn_summary: 这张1965年的专辑处于约翰·柯川四重奏从经典后波普向自由爵士过渡的关键节点，乐评人强调传统歌曲形式与柯川日益狂野探索之间的张力。《Chim Chim Cheree》开场即模仿《My Favorite Things》的模式，但柯川不到一分钟便开始挣脱旋律束缚，与鼓手琼斯一起冲破钢琴手泰纳的固定和弦循环。《Brazilia》和《Nature Boy》则预示了即将到来的解构式探索，将歌曲形式像膨胀的气球般撑到极限。乐评特别指出同期Half Note的现场录音显示这些曲目在现场被拉长至两倍长度，揭示了录音室版本中被压缩的实验冲动。Impulse厂牌发行，柯川四重奏——柯川、泰纳、琼斯、加里森——的标准配置在传统框架内孕育着即将爆发的自由爵士革命。

items.body: John Coltrane – Live at the Village Vanguard (Impulse, 1997) By Kenneth Blanchard There are certain recordings that stretched my grasp of jazz (and indeed music). Andrew Hill’s Point of Departure comes to mind. Coltrane’s LVV collection is another. Recorded over four nights in 1961 at the Jerusalem of Jazz, only five of the originally recorded numbers were released in the following two years. The 1997 box set is a genuine treasure. The structure of the music remains within standard hop bop spaces, but the moods blossom into an entirely new ecosystem. The inclusion of Eric Dolphy was one of Trane’s most brilliant moves. On Naima, Spiritual, India , his low horns (also sax and bass clarinet) perfectly match Trane’s tenor and soprano sax. Trane’s interest in alternative spiritual and musical traditions is obvious enough. His famous “sheets of sound” slide in and out of every line. I find the articulation of Coltrane’s own personality to be as vivid here as on any of his recordings. Email This BlogThis! Share to X Share to Facebook
items._cn_summary: 这张1997年发行的套装收录了1961年Coltrane在Village Vanguard四晚演出的录音，原版仅释出五首，此盒装完整呈现了当时未被发行的素材。Eric Dolphy的低音管与中音萨克斯在此加入，与Coltrane的次中音和高音萨克斯形成独特对话。作品结构虽植根于bebop语汇，但情绪与氛围已延伸至全新的音乐生态，体现出Coltrane对非西方精神与音乐传统的探索。评论特别指出其'sheets of sound'技法在此展现出鲜明的个人特质，是理解Coltrane艺术转折的重要现场文献。

items._cn_summary: 意大利三人组 Nuhara 的首张专辑 Rama 尝试将西西里口头民俗传统与当代电子音乐相融合，体现出明确的跨界意识。乐团从地方民间音乐档案中提取素材，借助电子手段对民俗旋律与节奏进行重新编排，使口头传统在合成器与采样语境中获得了新的呈现方式。从现有描述来看，专辑并非简单附加电子音色，而是试图建立传统与现代之间的结构性对话，这与其「fearlessly original」的定位相符。该项目对民俗素材的当代转化路径具有探讨价值，为世界音乐与电子实验的交叉地带提供了一个来自南欧地区的样本。

items.body: Review by siLLy puPPy — Drone music is nothing new of course having existed in ancient musical forms ranging from ancientHindustani and Carnatic styles to Japanese gagaku, Byzantine chants and Scottish bagpipes however interms of more modern Western music it really got a foothold in the early world of electronic musicwhen La Monte Young began a new minimalist experimentalism that has continued to the current day. Bythe late 60s acts like Finland's The Sperm and Germany's Kluster soon to be Cluster as well aslesser known artists like Italy's Harry Bertoia were really warming up to the possibilities of darkambient sounds set to a sustained note. A handful of acts began to follow suit however oneinteresting artifact from the early 70s was the album PLANES by the duo of GREGOR C�RTEN & ANSEMROGMANS who only entered the musical arena to record this sole album before C�RTEN would move on tothe world of visual art and painting while ROGMANS would become a school teacher and choir director.For having no prior history and no future releases, PLANES is a surprisingly cool album that fitright into the burgeoning progressive electronic and Krautrock sweeping the German music scene ofthe era. This album came out in 1974 and featured two sprawling tracks that each swallowed up anentire side of the vinyl release. Following in the footsteps of Kluster, Eliane Radigue and La MonteYoung, GREGOR C�RTEN & ANSEM ROGMANS crafted a haunting display of electronically hypnotic dronefreakiness that seemed to be part Kluster, part early Klaus Schulze and part A.R. & Machines. Whiledrone music is hit and miss with most acts missing the mark of what it takes to deliver attentionkeeping minimalism that can sustain an album's worth of material, PLANES is an interesting rarityfrom the era that offers a nice escapist's paradise into a sonic playground that finds just enoughspices to keep it all enthralling.The first side simply titled "Planes I" sounds like a musical shaving session with a buzzing soundthat sounds like an electric razor that establishes itself a good while before haunting wordlessvocalizations and creepy organs find themselves embellished by a series of random electronic effectsand tape manipulations. While the droning effects are in the forefront, the tenebrous organ riffsand lugubrious vocals are quite chilling as the track slowly drifts through its 18-minute plusduration. The contemplative buzzing mediation adds that certain uneasiness while the pacifyingpredictability simultaneously soothes the soul. The second track titled "Planes II" offers a totallydifferent spin albeit in a similarly themed droning drift that also lasts just slightly longer thanthe 18-minute mark. This one opens with a tinny repetitious guitar twang that slowly changes pitchup and down the scale and then joined in by a slow monotonous organ drone that also incrementallyflows glacially. This particular effect is very much out of the Achim Reichel playbook but yetsounds totally unique in this context. Drone music can be quite dull if not done properly but these guys really knew how to generate analbum's worth of exhilarating drone music by creating a fascinating slow building tension that couldhave been one of the inspirations of the later post-rock. The album artfully incorporates the tonesand flavors of progressive electronic, especially the Berlin School variety along with Krautrocktechniques only funneled into a more minimalist drone style of slowly unfolding musical innovations.The production is very good and the album is best experienced loud and on a good speaker where youcan feel the reversing micro-changes of the pitches which offer an entire body experience. It's aninteresting underground relic of Germany's fertile musical underground and one that shouldn't bemissed by lover's of electronic escapist music. While Kluster is the most brandished reference, thismusic isn't nearly as bleak and industrial sounding and more detached in a creepy drugged outexperience way.
items._genre: drone / progressive electronic / krautrock / dark ambient
items._cn_summary: 这张1974年的专辑由Gregor Cörten与Anselm Rogmans合作完成，仅此一张便退出乐坛。作品包含两首各占据唱片一面的长篇作品，延续了La Monte Young、Kluster等先驱的极简主义电子嗡鸣路线。第一首以类似电动剃须刀的持续嗡鸣声为基础，叠加阴森的管风琴与无人声唱诵，缓慢漂移超过十八分钟。第二首则以细薄重复的吉他拨弦开场，配合单调管风琴长音缓缓推进，带有Achim Reichel式的音色处理却又自成一格。整张专辑在持续低音与催眠式循环中构建出幽暗的声景空间，将早期电子嗡鸣、暗黑氛围与德国实验摇滚传统融为一体。作为该时期罕见的独立创作，其声音探索在同类作品中呈现出相当的完成度与沉浸感。

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — In the early 1980s, German musician Peter Frohmader, creator of the famous Nekropolis trilogy, teamed up with none other than Artemiy Artemiev. Like Frohmader, Artemiev was an electronic musician, but he was also the son of Eduard Artemiev, a pioneer of Russian electronic music who had composed, among other works, the soundtrack for Andrei Tarkovsky's film Solaris.Here, each playing a synthesizer, they weave a subtle sonic tapestry; utilizing electric guitar, bass, and gong percussion, Frohmader shapes a progressive symphony that evokes the "space rock" era of Pink Floyd, the psychedelia of the band Gong, and the harmonic style of Klaus Schulze. What makes the work novel and original is the way guitar variations play against synthesizer loops, much like an overcast sky filled with countless clouds, where rays of light occasionally break through the monochromatic sheen, tearing the canvas here and there to complete the panorama. Hints of rock and blues emerge, improvisations set against the unwavering electronic foundations, creating a truly unique texture.Later on, it takes on a percussive intensity as the guitar launches into psychedelic jams, almost as if Steve Hillage had stepped onto the scene, and the term "electronic progressive rock" acquires a new meaning; the fusion becomes even more deeply intertwined in "Space Icon." "Mir" is the second track; in Russian, it means "Peace," but it can also signify "Universe" or "World." This double meaning, this duality, suits the track's music perfectly; in contrast to the expansive opening, the sound is relaxed, mysterious, and introspective. Electronic music evokes sensations and moods that are not always associated with words, at least not initially, yet it is that secondary level of meaning that we are attempting to explore here.Once again, layered synthesizers and gongs serve an ethereal melody that seems to evoke the presence of a hidden soprano, while "Channeling", the third track, is more tribal, primitive, organic, and minimalist; it calls to mind the East and reminded me of Brand X's percussion, as Frohmader actually plays fretless bass on this track. Turning to the East, "Zen Garden" fully immerses us in that realm; one can picture Pierre Moerlen and his percussion work with Gong, yet set within a context where everything seems to float. The synthesizers resemble currents of wind, and simultaneously pan flutes, reinforcing a sense of earthly connection. "Space Icon" orbits between these two poles: the earthly realm and the space beyond Earth."Cosmic Jungle" is an expansive closing track that fuses the jungle and the cosmos; it gradually becomes saturated with dissonance as the sounds of birds morph into tribal drums, contrasting sharply with those distinctly electric dissonances, before circling back to the minimalism of the opening, ultimately concluding with an ambient finish reminiscent of Delia Derbyshire and the Standard Music Library.Recorded between Art Recording Studio in Moscow and Studio Nekropolis in Munich, this collaborative album culminates in a projection of Russo-German influences that stands as an icon of that very fusion.
items._genre: progressive electronic / space rock / ambient / experimental fusion
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑由德国电子音乐家Peter Frohmader与俄罗斯电子先驱Artemiy Artemiev合作完成，两人以合成器为核心，融合电吉他、无品贝斯与锣等打击乐器，构建出层次丰富的渐进式电子音景。评论将其比作Pink Floyd式的太空摇滚与Gong乐队的迷幻风格，同时具备Klaus Schulze的谐波特质。吉他即兴段落与合成器循环的交织形成核心张力，电子节拍之上不时浮现摇滚与蓝调的暗示。第三轨走向部落化、极简主义的东方冥想氛围，竖琴般合成器与风声般的铺底塑造出漂浮感；终曲则将丛林声响与宇宙音景相融合，鸟类鸣叫变形为部落鼓点，最终回归到Delia Derbyshire式的环境音乐收束。整体呈现出一种地球与太空之间的双极对话。

items.body: Review by Stroumpf — Imbued with post metal and symphonic movements cores of death, black and abstract math metal fuse in a Large Orgone Collider -a showcase of overpowering inventiveness and technical bravuraStephen Jarrett's despondent, hyper-agile, 'psychological' guitar narrates and nervously navigates the manic, fluctuating surreal world of external horrors it builds: a landscape of dread and overwhelming doom textures to simulate a complete eclipse. As sonic, technically overpowering dramaturge, master-narrator and litterateur withing the distinct sub-genre of abstract tech metal, he shares an astonishing conceptual and technical lineage with Robert Fripp and Steve Hackett.With a melancholy anthropomorphic elephant holding a mandolin on the album cover (and who does not know that African forest elephants disperse the seeds of the ebony trees from which premium guitar fingerboards are made), one is likely to think of a surreal Jazz festival poster. 'Jazzy' and surreal in an abstract tech death metal way, linear through-composed the ride is going to be, starting with an instrumental accelerando that could be an after-thought to The Goliath's 'Vomited Hyacinths'. The album asserts its individuality with the titular second track 'Joyless Parson' which forms together with the razor-sharp Slayer-esque head cleaner 'Mourn' (an instant classic of furious beastliness) and the monolithic 'The Void of course' (Voc) -a non-formulaic center piece and multi-movement epic- the three pillars of this piece of avant-guard art.With the analytical prose-anti-poetry telling us about the wretched and tortured joyless parson, who is kept alive by a contemptuous life force, his pastoral illusions ('fantastic lies worth repeating' up until his 'feeling unworthy of pleasure [?] guarding alone a cache of treasure which no one values and no one visits'), there seems not much space for emotional growth: nevertheless, the musical representation of a hypnotic decent into human depravity and existential paralysis offers us a breath-taking juxtaposition of intense mathematical dissonance and serene, sorrowful classical melodicism and haunting chamber melancholy (piano and cello) prefiguring their 2024 masterwork 'Pleroma'. Abandon expectations of genre-typical, traditional metal anthems with refrains along a uniform hyper-fast blast beats-driven grid (though Orgone can do anthemic, world-shattering riffs and head-banging stuff, too). The guitar work (and the guitar does all the work) centers on non-repeating distinct upper register micro-phrases -shall we call them micro-riffs or 'micro-memes?'-, each bar organically and erratically mutating into the next. The ever-shape-shifting guitar work will mimic and impressively dramatize how a hapless individual racks his brain. Layers of Black Sabbath DNA lie bare: knotty, sludgy riffage, almost minimalistic, primitive playing style and muddy mid-range crunch make appearances. But it's Tony Iommi on amphetamines: everything is shot through, imbued and augmented with expressive, breathtakingly inertia-free fretboard swash-buckling, rapid-fire interval leaps, chaotic chromatic shifts, attacking pushing micro-timing driving the beast, counter-melodic playing and harsh dissonances. Jarrett's anti-traditional soloing is existential protagonist, agitator, catalyst and jumpingly associative propellant. Beside itself in a mental flow, it is its own antagonist, commenting, probing, cajoling, shooting distracting flares; it falters and picks itself up again, flays the strings, wields justice on the hoof, runs evasive maneuvers, inserts evocative moments of respite and serenity expanding with soaring climaxes of staggering beauty (again and non-repetitively again). The guitar work literally whips and drags the band along, until heights of despair turn into blazing technical and melodical fireworks.'Void of course', an astrological term apparently refers to the moon's transitioning between Zodiac signs and its running into emptiness symbolizes a time of [self-imposed] isolation. The 14 min long song serves as the album's emotional and sonic anchor. Much of JP's runtime is therefore spent in sinuous, drifting fluctuations, patient, lumbering builds, a suffocating crawl forming heavy, expansive doom and echoey post metal atmospheres before straight-ahead aggression strikes again up to successions of disorienting peripeties, drawn-out climaxes and releases, culminating in some grotesque dance of the near-dead and a very painfully evocative, psychotic Caspar Br�tzmann-like pingy, plinky-ploink disintegration fest. A heart-breaking atmospheric drop into a mental chasm follows with a shuddersome coda. Most guitarists would have exhausted and repeated their vocabulary of tricks and phrases several songs ago. Multi-instrumentalist and ego-free gentleman shredder Jarrett, however, up to the messy, slightly fuzzy, synoptic round-up track 'Circulated Treason' that even contains slivers of uplifting, playful music, he just keeps on giving. As the architect of its own nightmare, he layers chaotic, multi-tracked arpeggios that are like structural fractures. Drummer Justin Wharton utilizes staccato shifts, sudden stops and accelerations to sound out the psychological load with servings of disorienting time-signatures and something akin to American Primitivism while (even) the deft vocal delivery adds vocal percussion, atmosphere and inimitable lyrical heft.'Joyless Parson' is bleaker, more doom-laden and was recorded only 1 year after its equally inspired, very, very fast predecessor 'The Goliath'. The slowing down allows breathing space for the instruments and incredible skills to shine. Together they stand closer to the brain-frying, punishing mathcore debut 'Accumulator' than to the multi-voiced, genre-fluid, maximalist super production 'Pleroma' [2024] though the idioms, and symphonic sweep are already manifest.Oh well, the album lacks a bit of sound engineering clarity (especially compared to the follow-up 'Pleroma') -but so what? Hey, we know what it is meant to sound like and that's all that matters! An utterly uncompromising 96%

items.body: Review by siLLy puPPy — One of the most unique and stranger acts to emerge from the 70s prog scene was bizarre in many waysactually. AKASHA emerged from Norway, a nation currently prolific to progressive music in the 21stcentury wasn't a major player in the golden years of prog rock. And this band didn't come from Oslo,This short-lived act came from one of the most northern regions of all of Europe and formed in thesmall Arctic fishing village of Kj�llefjord. But what makes this band strange is that it reallydidn't sound like any other act of the day despite smatterings of influences piled into the schizoidrandom musical styles that seemed to find bits and pieces derived from Genesis, Pink Floyd, TheMoody Blues and King Crimson amongst others. The band was a quintet featuring Sverre Svendsen onlead vocals and mellotrons, Jens Ivar Andreassen on guitars, Mellotron, synthesizers, piano, organ,Arild Andreassen on bass, Kjell Evensen on drums and also included are the lyrics and poetry of Tor-Jony Hansen. AKASHA released only one mere album in 1977 and given its extreme remote location with littleopportunity for promotion or touring for that matter, the album has become one of those extremerarities. The strange artifact is also unique in that it displays the track listings on the frontcover but what really sets this one apart is the mishmash of music sounds that include hypnoticspace rock, freaky sound generated through synthesizers and mellotrons and a schizophrenic hairpinpropensity to simply morph into other music styles midstream reminding me a bit of the GermanKrautrock act Silberbart albeit with less guitar bombast. Likewise the band recorded in a bomb-proofcellar which was used as a shelter in the basement of a hotel in the small town of Finnsnes, Norwaywhich gives the production an interesting uniqueness much in the way of the band German Oak whichrecorded in a similar bomb shelter.The lengthy "Isle Of Kawi" begins the epic journey sounding something like the French Archaĩa withrapid fire synthesized arpeggios and what sounds like some sort of folk music but then sort ofshifts gears and sounds a bit more like something Pulsar would've conjured up on the first tworeleases. With this opening track it feels like you've stumbled into some lost classic musical treatas the sonic display is brooding and dark and on par with early Univers Zero for apocalyptic motifsof complete detachment from established paradigms. The track continues to morph into a labyrinthinedisplay of interesting twists and turns. The album quickly reveals its greatest flaw though on thesecond track "Bondage" which finds the lackluster vocal style of Sverre Svendsen who delivers arather mopey scatter-brained performance over some sort of drugged out lounge music before the trackbursts into rapid-fire key arpeggios that prognosticate the work of Philip Glass on "Glassworks" andhis classic "Koyaanisqatsi." And then off to some early "Trespass" styled Genesis sounding prog!The instrumental combo effect of "Recitativ" and "Electronic Nightmare" displays the band at itsmost unhinged with the first track in full rock mode for the first time only with strange guitarriffs and off-kilter contrapuntal elements. Unlike the prior tracks, this one has pounding drums anda guitar solo. The second on the other hand goes into outer space and features avant-gardeexperimentalism carried out through overlayering electronic effects sounding more Tangerine Dream orKlaus Schulze with a steady rhythmic pulse of Jean Michel Jarre. "Death Hymn" combines faster rockwith the electronics and then breaks into some sort of rockin' the classics keyboard freneticismmore in vein of The Nice. But wait! There's more - it then morphs into a slow oozing space rockmotif with detached spoken word lyrics which are in English. "Light And Darkness" is one of the mostschizoid tracks with several changes of tempos, styles and rich in off-kilter time signatures andjust plain bonkers ideas. More steeped in rock but drenched in mellotrons and atmospheric weirdnessas well."The Trip" offers the most normal track on board and actually sticks to a bluesy rock format formost of its run however the closing "Man And The Void" however returns to the restless nature of thealbum with a space rock intro that quickly shifts into strange guitar chord riffs and at timesreminds me of Gnidrolog but less structured and more freeform in many ways. This album offers thetrue spirit of DIY musical ambitions overcoming the extreme remote geography, lack of recordingfacilities and production extravaganzas. This band truly did things its own way on its own terms.Despite the imperfections of weak vocals, lackluster production and blatant disregard for any sortof unified sound, this album will appeal to those seeking out the most unapologetically originalalbums of the era and despite the flaws more than makes up for in its sheer creative audacity thatmakes AKASHA really a difficult band to classify with its symphonic prog, Krautrock and eclecticmusic spirit. For my tastes this one is quite appealing.

items.body:
The brotherhood of foundational European avant garde bassists gets smaller with each passing year. And among those still living, some are either inactive for various reasons or working in other fields, musical or otherwise. So, the subset of ones still going is a small but precious list.

Among them is the Netherlands’ Arjen Gorter. Ask even a relatively informed listener of European avant garde jazz about him and almost invariably the first association will be Willem Breuker, and more specifically his Kollektief. Gorter did anchor that group for the entirety of its existence (1975-2010, with a retrospective farewell tour coming after Breuker’s death) alongside drummer Rob Verdurmen, allowing Breuker and a rotating cast of string and horn players (though trombonist Bernard Hunnekink was another stalwart) to navigate complex and subversive music, confident that a strong foundation would always support them. But like Jimmy Cobb always being referenced first and sometimes only as the last living participant of Kind of Blue after Miles Davis died in 1991, Gorter’s career, still ongoing, is hardly exclusive to his work with Breuker.

Gorter was born in Amsterdam on January 2nd, 1948 and he has resided in the Dutch capital his whole life. His road to the bass was a circuitous one. As he wrote in an email, “I liked the accordion when I was very young. It was common in the Amsterdam streets of the ‘50s, but the tunes that my teacher made me play were too silly, so that did not last. My dad imported musical instruments. He brought a slightly damaged ukulele home and so at around 11 I tried playing along with the nightly jazz broadcasts on French and Belgian radio. The father of a friend had a small jazz collection and I loved the Art Blakey Blue Note 45s, the Monk LP and the other stuff he had. So that ukulele was replaced by a guitar. I started jamming in our attic with friends and others and at some point someone brought a double bass upstairs and left it there for six months. I had fun playing it and managed to buy it from him once he showed up again.”

During high school Gorter played guitar in a band for school dances, repertoire ranging from period rock tunes to jazz compositions. He began college in 1966, aiming to study political science and sociology, the same year he first worked professionally with Breuker, having heard the older reed player’s bands around town and once playing with him at a jam session. Gorter was invited to join a new Breuker group, which performed at the Loosdrecht Jazz Competition as a sextet, then expanded to almost two-dozen musicians for the final stage. This group would make Litany for the 14th of June 1966 (Relax) in late October 1966, Gorter’s recording debut alongside two other bassists, the much older Dick van der Capellen and Victor Kaihatu.

Gorter would balance university and performing for a few years. During this time, he would work with Germany’s Gunter Hampel, appearing on his April 1968 Wergo date Gunter Hampel Group + Jeanne Lee and participating in the November 1968 Total Music Meeting in Berlin, where photo evidence has him in a bizarre encounter with Hampel, John McLaughlin, Sonny Sharrock, Pharoah Sanders, Roy Ayers, Laurie Allan, and Roel Kroes. 1969 saw even more activity: more Hampel work, including the album The 8th of July 1969 (inaugurating his Birth imprint); playing on German trumpeter Manfred Schoof’s FMP release European Echoes and being part of the Peter Brötzmann Oktett at the International Holy Hill Jazz Meeting (alongside Buschi Niebergall and Peter Kowald; Richard Williams’ review of European Echoes in the March 14th, 1970 issue of Melody Maker saying, “It’s an astonishingly powerful performance, with particularly superb work by Dudek, Bailey and the three basses, who play a really fantastic trio section.”). Gorter is also heard on the Live at The Bohemia Jazzclub recording by Hans Dulfer’s Soulbrass Inc., as well as a track with Breuker and Han and Peter Bennink heard on the Instant Composers Pool cheese box. As Gorter recalled, “I managed to juggle both activities until the end of 1969, but I was more on the road than in Amsterdam and had to make a choice and I chose the activity that gave me way more satisfaction.”

During the first half of the ‘70s, Gorter and Breuker did not work together often, at least as can be gleaned from available recordings: Hampel’s People Symphony (Birth, 1970) and part of his group that participated in German avant garde composer Hans Werner Henze’s Der Langwierige Weg In Die Wohnung Der Natascha Ungeheuer; and an unofficial Amsterdam recording from 1973 under Breuker’s leadership and a live date from Leo Cuypers in 1974, both with groups prefiguring the Kollektief (Cuypers was its first pianist). Otherwise Gorter was busy – again, at least on record – with Hans Dulfer, Kees Hazevoet, Theo Loevendie, Alexander Von Schlippenbach, and the Irène Schweizer-Rüdiger Carl Quartet. The latter two were significant. Gorter was part of the second iteration of Schlippenbach’s Globe Unity Orchestra, Niebergall and Kowald in tow once more (a 1970 Berlin Jazz Festival performance released in 2001) and the Schweizer-Rüdiger Carl group that was active for several years. “I met Rudiger in Wuppertal, that was a new jazz center by itself thanks to Peter Brötzmann and Peter Kowald,” wrote Gorter. “Sometimes I stayed at the studio that he shared with guitar wizard Hans Reichel. When Irene and Rudiger started playing together, they asked me to join and we played many places in the early ‘70s, with Heinrich Hock, Louis Moholo, or Alan Bateman on drums.” That band made only one full album, 1974’s Goose Pannée (FMP) but did have a track on the For Example - Workshop Freie Musik 1969 - 1978, the FMP boxed set.

1974-75 was an important period for two other reasons. Besides the aforementioned collaborations as well as work with the Boy Edgar Big Band and the small groups of Maurice Horsthuis and Toon van Vliet, Gorter was one of the musicians who helped establish Amsterdam’s Bimhuis, ultimately one of Europe’s premier venues for avant garde music, performing on its October 1st, 1974 opening night with the Burton Greene Quartet. Then in March 1975, Breuker asked Gorter to be a member of his Kollektief. Gorter described the group’s music as such: “Willem’s music had a lot of freedom. There were often tightly arranged written sections that would suddenly end and then the fun was to play on as if the arrangement continued – there was usually no such thing as chord changes – or to let the thing fall off a cliff ... Anyway, the music always felt fresh to play, even after many concerts, and there was a great mix of individual input and group discipline and cooperation. The Kollektief’s music linked the recognizable to the unexpected, often in 90-degree turns. It was surprising but accessible. For us musicians there was a wide spectrum of activities, from theater plays to movie music to interpretations of classical music and a lot of traveling to places where we found appreciative audiences, ranging from Australian school children to Chinese businessmen.”

The Kollektief would go on to make over three dozen albums, mostly released on Breuker’s BV Haast label, and perform all over the world, including during the Klap op de Vuurpijl (roughly, Top It All Off) Festival, taking place over five days at the end of each year from 1976-2005. Its book mixed Breuker and other band member pieces with tunes from various pages of the Great American Songbook and drawn from the classical canon, as well as other sources, presented in a highly theatrical manner best appreciated live and mixing in humor in refreshing contrast to the dour stage demeanor of many an improviser.

As busy as the Kollektief would keep him, Gorter still pursued other projects, some including fellow Kollektief members, including Breuker, and only existing on stages, such as groups under the leadership of Maarten van Norden, Sean Bergin, Boy Raaymakers, Pierre Courbois, Nedly Elstak, Jasper van ‘t Hof, Misha Mengelberg, and others. A representative sampling of those can be found in the archive of the Bimhuis (https://www.bimhuis.nl/archief); when he was in Amsterdam, this would be Gorter’s home near his home.

But there were also ones documented as albums: Maine, the 1975 collaboration of American trombonist Roswell Rudd with Dulfer, Gorter, and drummer Martin van Duynhoven, was made up of music by Sonny Rollins and Rudd (who had been coming to and working in the Netherlands since the mid ‘60s both with the New York Art Quartet and also locals like Loevendie). There were two 1977 dates by Cuypers, Zeeland Suite also including another bassist in South African expatriate Harry Miller; the 1979 Maarten Van Norden/Boy Raaymakers quartet date Chicken Song, completed by drummer Peter Nykyruj (of Mike Osborne fame); and a pair of 1980 albums spearheaded by the aforementioned trumpeter/composer Elstak (and released on his Coreco label; Gorter had loosely studied harmony with him in the ‘60s): To Build was led by Soesja Citroen’s name, who was one of five singers alongside Elstak, Breuker, Gorter, and Van Duynhoven for Sad Trumpets. The most significant, at least in terms of international exposure, came in July 1984, when Gorter, Mengelberg, and Bennink joined forces with two Americans, soprano saxophonist Steve Lacy and trombonist George Lewis, for the Soul Note release Change of Season (Music Of Herbie Nichols). Another important recording came 13 years later with Legendary: The 27th of May 1997, in a reunion with Hampel, who was fêting his seminal Heartplants SABA album from 1965 with original participants Courbois, Schlippenbach, and Schoof, Gorter standing in for his late friend Buschi Niebergall. One interesting takeaway from this is that it is often thought that after Breuker split with his fellow Instant Composers Pool founders Mengelberg and Bennink there were two distinct worlds in Dutch avant garde jazz; however, there were musicians like Gorter who operated in both spheres.

The new millennium found Gorter in several new projects: the mostly American blues/jazz band New Texas Swing from American saxophonist and then fellow Kollektief member Alex Coke with singer Tina Marsh and drummer John Betsch; the aptly named though horn-heavy Drummers Double Bill from Arend Niks and Verdurmen; 2000 recording The Compositions Of Eric Dolphy (BV Haast) with Coke, Breuker, Eric Vloeimans, Frank van Bommel, and John Engels; and Bo Van De Graaf’s I Compani; and the Rahsaan Roland Kirk “tribute” band Reeds & Deeds, also put together by Van De Graaf.

The Dolphy project had a personal resonance for Gorter, more specifically a much younger version of himself. In 1964, when he was 16, Gorter attended the Charles Mingus Sextet performance at Amsterdam’s Concertgebouw, a band with Dolphy, Johnny Coles, Clifford Jordan, Jaki Byard, and Dannie Richmond, which Gorter calls “the best ever ... Halfway through a trumpet solo by Johnny Coles, Eric left the stage while playing and walked into the hall. He ended up right next to my seat, way in the back. For a 16-year-old, that may have been a life-changing experience.” In 2011, Gorter was given the opportunity to celebrate Dolphy once more with a concert at the Bimhuis: “Eric Dolphy at The Five Spot Revisited,” with the legendary recording’s repertoire played by himself, Tom Arthurs, Rudi Mahall/Alex Coke (as his bass clarinet and saxophone/flute sides), Benoît Delbecq, and John Betsch.

Gorter joined the multimedia ensemble I Compani, founded by Van De Graaf in 1985, in 2010. As he wrote, “Bo van de Graaf just called it quits for I Compani, which I understand but regret. He led that band for 40 years through great adventures and I was happy to participate since 2010 or so. If anyone is comparable to Breuker in the amount of initiatives he took, it is him. Original pieces are blended with film music and live video, in various lineups from septet to 18-piece band. His music has the space, freedom and versatility of Breuker’s, but in a different way. Fun!”

When asked about the European scene in which he came up, Gorter replied, “At that time every European city had a very original and recognizable improvised music scene, or a few of them, like London with both the Spontaneous Music Ensemble and Brotherhood of Breath,” he wrote. “And they all had international contacts and were sharing with each other. So, the originality of these approaches, and the mutual respect, encouraged the exchange between countries and scenes and the musicians and their supporters took the initiative to made it happen.”

As for his own methodology towards, as shown in this piece, the variety of musical situations in which he has taken part, Gorter spoke both simply and profoundly: “From the beginning I played both free improvisation and tunes based on chord changes. Learning on stage was an option in the ‘60s, which sometimes led to embarrassment but more often to improvement. My approach is: first try to play what you hear, then figure out what others call it (= music theory), then apply that to play better what you hear and so on. Nowadays much education starts on the second step ...”

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑聚焦荷兰低音提琴演奏家Arjen Gorter的音乐生涯，既涵盖他作为Willem Breuker Kollektief乐队核心成员的漫长合作（1975-2010），也追溯了他从阿姆斯特丹少年时期由手风琴、尤克里里、吉他逐步走向低音提琴的曲折经历。文章回顾了他1966年与Breuker初次合作的录音首作Litany for the 14th of June 1966，以及与德国自由爵士萨克斯手Gunter Hampel的合作。作为欧洲前卫爵士的根基性人物，Gorter的低音线条在复杂而颠覆性的作曲结构中提供了稳固支撑。文章以传记叙事为主，穿插历史背景与乐队编制细节，适合对欧洲自由即兴场景感兴趣的听众深入了解这位常被低估的低音提琴手的全貌。

items.body:
There is a substantial list of attributes that sets Ran Blake apart from every other innovative pianist of the past sixty-plus years, each of which falls under one of two headings: his choice of materials and his treatments of them. The former is based on Blake’s ability to hear connections between materials for which “disparate” is an inadequate descriptor. Who else would sequence Max Roach’s “Mendacity” and “Saving All My Love for You” – or “On Top of Old Smokey” and Michel Legrand’s “Watch What Happens”? Nobody, because what Blake does is unique. He doesn’t interpret materials as much as administer an MRI, revealing the connective tissues and vital organs as vividly, if not more so, than the skeletal structure. In the process, Blake makes the familiar sound radically new.

Blake’s collaborations with singers are central to his work. The current critical consensus is that his groundbreaking work with Jeanne Lee overshadows everything since, the respective qualities of notables like Christine Correa and Sara Serpa notwithstanding. Roots & Byways circumvents the edifice The Newest Sound Around has become, primarily because Dominique Eade takes a different tact. She is not as rooted as Correa – or Lee, for that matter – in Billie Holiday, and she is not as committed to understatement as Serpa. Like both Correa and Serpa, Eade can shape a song syllable by syllable and render a highly personal interpretation. It is Eade’s palpably deep joy in singing that sets her apart, one that is not only bursting at the seams on showstoppers like the Whitney Houston megahit, but one that even seeps into noirish songs like Mingus’ “Portrait.” It is the key to her relatability and appeal, and to that of the album, as well.

items._cn_summary: 兰·布莱克与多米尼克·伊德合作的《Roots & Byways》聚焦钢琴与人声的极端解构与重组。布莱克以独到的材料选择著称，将马克斯·罗奇、Michel Legrand等风格迥异的作品并置，揭示其内在关联而非表面联系，其手法被形容为对乐曲施以核磁共振扫描，使熟悉旋律焕发全新面貌。专辑延续布莱克与歌手合作的核心脉络，但伊德区别于此前合作过的Jeanne Lee、Christine Correa与Sara Serpa——她对Billie Holiday传统的依赖更少，也并不执着于含蓄表达，而是凭借逐音节雕琢歌词的能力与歌唱时溢出的深层欢愉形成辨识度。这种喜悦既体现在惠特尼·休斯顿式的大歌段落，也渗透于 Mingus 的暗色调曲目《Portrait》，构成专辑的情感基调与亲和力来源。整体呈现出学院派爵士框架内对曲目编排与演唱美学的个人化实验。

items.body: Documenting Sound is a new tape and digital series from Boomkat Editions. Over time, they will release a number of recordings from a selection of artists, all from different parts of the globe and a wide range of musical disciplines. These pieces, made during the last couple of pandemic-hit months, offer a personal and intimate glimpse into the artist and their music. The only condition was that the music should be recorded at home or in its own surroundings, without too much in the way of pre-planning or thoughts surrounding its composition. As a result, the music is open and unexpected, going outside the box and wandering far, making this a series perfect for artistic exploration. Instead of presenting an impoverished viewpoint of lockdown, the pandemic has resulted in a creative explosion as artists and musicians livestream and record from home. Field recordings, found sounds, improvisation, spoken word, and song-writing were all encouraged, and this edition, entitled Gathers, features an hour of new music from Sarah Davachi, recorded at her home in Los Angeles in Spring 2020. ‘I’ve been going through various stages of movement – some days I can’t be motivated to do anything and other days I can spend long hours working on music and going deep into it. When I’ve been able to sit with making music, it’s been incredibly meaningful and reconfiguring for me at this moment. I’m thankful to have the time in my studio, a room that is calm and quiet and feels quite distant from the outside world, and this cassette is essentially a reflection of that interiorized state of being.’ ‘Gathers’ has grown out of two separate ideas and albums – one completed but as-yet-unreleased, and another currently in development. The improvised and unedited cassette can take the listener somewhere else even while they stay at home, becoming lost in the music, and Gathers feels both meditative and focused. The A side brings together harpsichord, harmonium, and piano. Sarah describes her harpsichord as being ‘my main instrument these past few weeks…these Renaissance tunings have such depth, a house of endless hallways, and it’s been great solace to disappear into them temporarily.’ These past few months have also disappeared, the strangely shaped and hazy afternoons erasing, time spooling as spring turns into summer, but they’ve also allowed connections to grow once again – connections and roots that have been severed or at least cut back by the demands of everyday life. The downtime has, perhaps, resulted in greater flexibility, opening introverted thoughts as people adjust to a more sedate way of life. In this recording, time is slipping; the quarantined music is the sound of a lie-in and a day that drags, but it also sounds focused, running deep. A session can become a deep-dive, and one can remain immersed for hours at a time. My synthesizers are like old friends. They were my first passion when I started collecting instruments, and this period of time has been a nice excuse to revisit some of them. Side B collects three electronic studies for Mellotron, electric organ, and synthesizer, which is combined with tape echo. Sarah describes them as her…’chosen electronic instruments, and the ones through which I’ve always found the highest degrees of stillness and transformation’. And that’s what this lockdown has done: not only a pause, but a cocoon in which a transformation has taken place, and from which the music has finally emerged, taking its first flight into a new and changed world. www.boomkat.com
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑是Boomkat Editions新推出的磁带与数字系列作品之一，收录了Sarah Davachi在2020年春季于洛杉矶家中录制的约一小时即兴音乐。专辑融合了拨弦键琴、管风琴与钢琴，A面集中呈现这几种乐器，使用文艺复兴调律体系，营造出深邃的声学空间感。B面涉及合成器，体现艺术家对早期电子乐器的长期热情。整张专辑未经过剪辑与预先规划，呈现出居家隔离期间沉思冥想的内向状态，时间感在音乐中被拉长与消解。作品体现了在缺乏外部刺激条件下，音乐家向内探索的创作路径，是一段关于独处、专注与声音沉浸的私密记录。

items.body: Blood Transmission is Dag Rosenqvist’s first solo album in three years. Welcome back! This is Dag in a thoughtful frame of mind; the notes are as sparse as an empty room, missing extravagant embellishments save for the necessary furniture. Everything is in order, uncluttered, highly organised, as if the music had suffered a visit from Marie Kondo and her never-ending checklist. Dag’s music does spark joy, but it’s restrained. Things are slow to get going (which is a good thing). A whipping wind jettisons into the atmosphere, freefalling into the track, and jagged, triangular synth-teeth burst up from the bedrock, taking clean bites out of the atmosphere with a nightmarish ferocity to match the shark in Jaws, whose naughty antics plagued the coastal town of Amity all those years ago. The danger is there – often hidden, concealing itself in the lower half of the sea’s horizontal divide – but it’s not shy to rise up and make your acquaintance when it wants to. Notes bubble up from the fathomless deep, and something is always building just beneath the track, the tension festooning around the outskirts of the track like an incoming headache. The pulsating heartbeat doesn’t let up; it keeps pumping and the legs keep on running, draining the battery and recording thousands of steps on its Fitbit. Blood Transmission is all about creating and destroying. Soft piano interludes seep into the cracks, while behemoth synths snap back in a vicious attack. It’s not an immediate threat: it comes at you from angles, with a Hadouken and a side-punch. Before you know it, the track is in the process of munching on aural take-out, a speedy devouring of the atmosphere it had first scented and then tracked and then attacked. Rolling synths avalanche and create an unstoppable force. Penultimate track ‘From Rivers to the Sea’ could have generated from a F*** Buttons album thanks to the heavy thumping of the beat and the electrocuted synth, forming a progression of raw and euphoric power, but quieter waters are never far away. Take the finale, ‘Absolutes’, which lands on a Queen-sized bed made of soft feathers. A piano comes to clean up the synth’s atrocity, daylight clearing away the debris. It’s another moment of renewal in an album that’s peppered with them. The piano is a steady stream, its water flowing like blood and its blood flowing like water. We’re gonna need a bigger boat. Blood Transmission by Dag Rosenqvist www.hiddenvibes.bandcamp.com
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑在稀疏与密集之间反复游走，以极简的音符布局构建出广阔的空间感。锐利的合成器音色如同尖齿从地基中破土而出，带有强烈的攻击性和不祥的压迫感；脉冲式节奏持续推进，底层暗流涌动，张力在乐曲边缘不断累积。钢琴作为间歇性的净化元素出现，与庞大的合成器形成对峙——破坏与重建的循环贯穿全作。编曲层次丰富但克制，每一处爆发都经过精心铺垫。专辑在暗黑氛围与内省时刻之间切换，最终以钢琴的清澈走向终结，形成从黑暗到光线的完整弧线。

items.body:
After the OĽUN album I reviewed enthusiastically a while back, here’s the next project, again motivated and led by violinist/fiddler/composer Ján Kružliak Jr., continuing the rapprochement, indeed embrace, between Slovakia’s traditional music and its classical music. This time it reconnects the works of classical composers who were inspired by and drew on village musics with those traditional sources and styles.
Three ensembles are involved: the Spectrum Quartett led by Kru�liak with two violins, viola and cello; Nogaband, the traditional-style quartet of fiddles, contra (chording viola) and bass that’s led by fiddler and singer Michal Noga; and the female vocal group Ulijanky, plus guest singer Simona Hulejov�.
The majority of the tracks are interpretations of works by Slovak composer Eugen Suchon (1908-1993), with others from fellow-Slovaks Ilja Zeljenka (1932-2007) and Alexander Moyzes (1906-1984), and Hungarian B�la Bart�k (1881-1945) who did a lot of his very detailed collecting of folk music in Slovakia.
In each case the sources - musicians and locations in villages across Slovakia - are credited in the notes, and these arrangements and performances reconnect with the energy and traditional vocal sound of those sources.
In no way is this an orchestra-smoothed thing; this is gutsy, brilliantly played and sung music with all the spirit, skill and technique of traditional music, from players and singers who deeply understand and inhabit it. It’s a glorious piece of work, music to luxuriate in. There’s too much richness to begin to detail, but here’s a dip into a few moments to give the flavor. The tracks all have very long titles detailing their sources, so for brevity’s sake I’ll just give track numbers.

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑由小提琴家兼作曲家Ján Kružliak Jr.主导，核心思路是将斯洛伐克传统民间音乐与古典音乐进行深度对接与重新融合，而非简单改编。三组乐队参与：弦乐四重奏Spectrum Quartett、传统弦乐四人组Nogaband及女声合唱团Ulijanky，外加客席歌手。曲目主要改编自斯洛伐克作曲家Eugen Suchoň、Ilja Zeljenka、Alexander Moyzes以及曾深入斯洛伐克采集民间音乐的匈牙利作曲家Béla Bartók的作品，每首曲目在唱片内页都标注了所引用的村落音乐人与采集地。演奏方式并非管弦乐化的平滑处理，而是保留传统音乐的粗粝感与能量，演奏者与歌手对传统音乐有深入理解与浸润感。传统声乐音色与古典作曲素材在此形成对话，构成一张兼具学术价值与田野质感的跨界作品。
